speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext: On motion of Hon. W. T. White (Minister of Finance) the order for the third reading of Bill No. 76, to supplement the revenue required to meet war expenditures, was discharged, and the House again went into committee on the Bill, Mr. Sevigny in the chair.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the amendment which I have to propose is to subsection 3 of section 20. It was called to my attention the other day that there might possibly be an abuse of the provisions of this section, under which we provide that action for the recovery of penalties may be taken in the name of the Minister of Finance, Minister of Inland Revenue, or in respect of penalties under Part 3, in the name of the Minister of Inland Revenue, or any other person. It was suggested that this might lead to litigation of a vexatious character. I have been impressed with the view put forward, and, while there is abundant precedent running through not only our own statutes but the statutes of the United Kingdom regarding the imposition of taxes justifying the language used, still, on account of the somewhat far-reaching character of this legislation, it has appeared advisable to the Government that the objection should be met and a modification made accordingly. I therefore have to submit the following amendment .*
Subsection 3, section 20, line 35, after the words "Part Two" insert the words "and Part Three," and at line 36 of the same subsection, after the words "Inland Revenue," strike out all the remainder of the subsection.
The section will then read as follows:
3. All penalties imposed by this Act may be sued for, prosecuted and recovered with costs by His Majesty's Attorney General of Canada, or, in respect of penalties under Part One, in the name of the Minister of Finance, or, in respect of penalties under Part Two, and Part Three, in the name of the Minister of Inland Revenue.

That will ensure that private individuals will not institute any prosecutions of a vexatious character.
Although the debate is, I believe, confined to the particular amendment which I mentioned in moving the resolution, I may be allowed to advert to another matter to which I promised to give consideration pending the third reading of this Bill. It relates to the International Postage Convention. The committee will recall that a question arose as to whether it would be necessary for the public to put an additional war stamp on letters where the postage is already five cents, which is the maximum postage referred to in the convention. I find that the Post Office Department has communicated with the International Bureau at Berne, and in reply it has been advised that letters and postal cards for international service cannot be subjected to any tax or fee or postal charge other than that which is established by the provisions of paragraph 1 section 12-I do not desire to discuss again the question of whether this is a tax or a postal charge. It makes no difference whether it is the one or the other. It is not open to the Government, without violation of the convention in question, to impose an additional tax or an additional postal charge. That is in substance what I stated to the committee the other day.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I certainly am of the opinion that the amendment which is now proposed ought to be favourably considered. This tax is a restriction, as all taxes are, upon the liberty of the subject. It is taking away from every one's revenue, and it may be abused. We know that all such taxes which bear a penalty are liable to be very seriously abused by a class of speculators who make it their duty to see that a man does not trespass beyond the law, and who take advantage of the opportunity if he does trespass. I approve the amendment, but I think my hon. friend would improve Tt IT Ee were to say:
All penalties imposed by this Act may be sued for, prosecuted and recovered with costs by His Majesty's Attorney General of Canada.
Why go beyond that? The amendment goes on to say:
Or in respect of penalty under Part 1, in the name of the Minister of Finance, or in respect of penalties under Part 2 and Part 3, in the name of the Minister of Inland Revenue.
The Attorney General, by reason of his office, is the one who should look after

infringements of the law.- It is not in the province of the Minister of Finance nor of the Minister of Inland Revenue to look after infringements of the law. That is the special duty conferred upon the Department of Justice. I cannot see any reason, and my hon. friend cannot give any good reason, why in one case the Attorney General should prosecute and in another, not the Attorney General, but a minister, should prosecute. My hon. friend is not able to give any good reason why there should be a departure from the principle to which I have referred, that is, that the Department of Justice is entrusted with looking after infringement of the law.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My right hon. friend has put forward the principle of uniformity. On account of my right hon. friend's long experience in legislation, I always treat any suggestions put forward By him with the greatest respect; but I will point out to him that in this amendment we are having regard absolutely to uniformity. My right hon. friend has overlooked the fact, or it has escaped his memory, that under the Inland Revenue Act, chapter 51, Revised Statutes, section 132, it is provided:
That every penalty Incurred for any offence against the provisions of this Act... if the amount or value of such penalty does not exceed $500, may be recovered or enforced by summary conviction under Part XV of the Criminal Code.
There is nothing in the Statute which says that information is to be laid by the Crown or under the authority of the Crown. Paley on Convictions, page 73, says:
Generally, any person may be an informer, but sometimes the statute governing the penalty allows only particular persons to inform.
The conclusion is, therefore, that any person may lay an information under the Inland Revenue Act for penalties recoverable by summary conviction.
Under the Inspection and Sale Act, chapter 85, Revised Statutes, section 45, it is provided that where the penalty or forfeiture exceeds $40, it may be sued for and recovered by any inspector, deputy inspector or any other person.
A somewhat different policy is provided by the Customs Act, section 266, which is as follows:
All penalties and forfeitures imposed by this Act or by any other Act relating to the customs or to trade or navigation shall, unless other provisions are made for the recovery thereof, be sued for, prosecuted and recovered
100J
with costs by His Majesty's Attorney General of Canada, or in the name of the Commissioner of Customs, or any officer or officers of customs, or other person or persons thereunto authorized by the Governor in Council, either expressly or by general regulation or orders, and by no other person.
In practice what I understand is done is this:	If the informer desires to lay an
information, he gives it to the Inland Revenue officer or officers, and prosecutions are then instituted. Therefore, so far as my hon. friend's exception or objection is founded upon the principle of uniformity, he will observe that we are strictly in accord with Dominion Statutes which have been in force for a number of years. There appears, therefore, no doubt that there is ample precedent, including the Inland Revenue Act itself, for the form of legislation here adopted of allowing a private individual to institute proceedings for a penalty; but in this particular case, for the reasons I have given, and in order that we may "avoid the possibility of vexatious litigation-I do not think that would have occurred-we have thought it well to lodge the right of prosecution only in a minister of the Crown. With that amendment to the Act, and in view of the fact that we are preserving, as I have stated, uniformity of the statutes, it would appear to me that the amendment that I have suggested would be quite ample to meet the objection raised by my right hon. friend.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: My hon. friend is doing the very reverse of what he says he is doing. He says he is putting in this amendment for the purpose of uniformity, and he refers to the Inland Revenue Act. That Act says that proceedings can be instituted by any informer. In this case the minister prevents the informer from laying information. Therefore, he diversifies, and then having taken from the Inland Revenue Act the power of having proceedings instituted by an informer, he refers US' again to that Act. The point is not worth fighting about; but it seems to me that, if this Government is to become a party to a suit, the only one who ought to become that party is the Attorney General. Yesterday, when the Militia Estimates were under consideration, 1 claimed that certain proprietors had not been paid for their land, and I w!as told that the matter was in the hands of the Attorney General. And so it ought to he. This legislation would be simplified if such matters were left in the hands of the Attorney General.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: When I spoke of uniformity, I quoted not only the Inland Revenue Act, but the Inspection and Sale Act, under which any penalty or forfeiture exceeding $40 may be sued for and recovered by any inspector, deputy inspector, or other person. I also referred to the Customs Act, under which the penalty may be recovered " by the Attorney General, or' in the name or names of the Commissioner of Customs, or any officers of the customs, or other person or persons thereunto authorized by the Governor in Council, either expressly or by general regulation or order, and by no other person." It was in reference to those statutes in particular that I spoke of uniformity. My right hon. friend, however, says the matter is not worth wasting any further time on.

Then, no prosecutions
could take place without the consent of the Attorney General?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Practically not without the
consent of the Attorney General.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

The Minister of Inland Revenue could dispense with tb? opinion of the Attorney General.
Mr. W'HITE: He would not do it.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
But he may.
Bill, as amended, reported, read the third time, and passed.

This accounts for the increase of $178,286.60 a year in the Estimates for the inside service. WTe can understand perfectly well that there are many more employees under the Government when we find that thirty-six additional buildings have been rented

since this Government came into power, and that they pay in rents no less than $178,000 a year more than their predecessors did. This is according to the figures furnished by the Minister of Public Works on the 15th and 22nd February last.
What is the total amount of the . rents paid by the Government in the city of Ottawa?

speakerposition: Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: The additional buildings rented by this Government represent an aggregate annual rental of $202,148.60; the leases expired represented rentals of a total of $23,880; leaving a balance, the net increase, of $178,268.60.
That is merely the increase ?

speakerposition: Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Yes.
The hon. member has not the total amount paid by the Government by way of salaries ?

speakerposition: Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: No; this is the increase in the total number of employees. The increase in connection with the cost of caring for the departmental buildings, which was $63,000 in 1911, is now $175,000. The Minister of Finance told us the other day, when this question of increase of civil servants was discussed, in an attempt to justify this increase, that in 1913 he had the greatest surplus in the history of this country. I understand that this year we will have the largest deficit that we have had, and according to the statement made by the Minister of Finance in his Budget speech, next year we may expect a larger one. The increase in the expenditure, according to the figures given by the hon. junior member for Halifax in his speech on the Budget, is over $6,000 a day for salaries alone. Under these circumstances, I think that if it is not possible to decrease the number of civil servants who are employed in the inside service in Ottawa, this is certainly not the time to increase it. I think that if my hon. friend's department finds it necessary to add to its staff, it should' obtain the necessary employees from other departments where their services may not be required.
How many employees are there in the inside service in my hon. friend's department ?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: There were 49 last year; next year there will be 52. This increase of three is because of our establishing the new naturalization branch which was provided for by the legislation passed la-1, year.
Have these appointments been made ?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: No.
The minister has not given any explanation of the enormous increase in the number of the employees in the inside service, and the consequent enormous outlay of money.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
I do not think
that I should be expected to give an explanation with respect to the increase in the other departments. The increase in the Department of the Secretary of State has not, I believe, been very large. We have had but few increases during the last three years. One of the reasons for the increase is that we have had to cope with a very large number of charters of incorporated companies; I am told that the number is much larger than it was during the preceding year. I am informed also by the officers of the department that the number of returns which it-has been necessary to prepare has exceeded that of previous years, and we have consequently had to add a few employees to the staff. Of course, in some of the other departments coming under the administration of the Secretary of State, increases have taken place; I can give the reasons for these increases when the Estimates for the departments concerned are brought before the committee.
Department of the Secretary of State-contingencies, $16,000.

What is the reason for
the increase of $5,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
This increase is rendered necessary by a general increase in the ordinary work of the department.
Mr. PUG8LEY: It'does seem to me that the hon. Secretary of State is not giving a fair and satisfactory reason for the increase for the coming year. These are times of declining revenue, and certainly at this period the minister should endeavour to reduce rather than increase the expenditure. As one hon. gentleman has said, there must he a large number of employees in other department? whose services are not required, and they could very well be transferred to the Department of the Secretary of State if additional help is required in that department. It cannot be true that with the collection of $30,000,000 or $40,000,000 lev-

than has been collected during the past two years, the same number of employees are required in the Customs Department. When we complain of the increased expenditure in these departments, and suggest that there should be a reduction, the answer is given that it would not be fair to the civil servants to dispense with their services. But why should they not be transferred? The work is largely clerical; in many cases it is the work of stenographers or clerks. If the Secretary of State wants additional help, why does he not go to the Minister of Customs and say: I want two or three clerks transferred to my department during the coming year; you do not require them, because you are collecting $30,000,000 or $40,000,000 less revenue than you collected in previous years. Is there any reason why that should not be done?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Even if they were transferred, I would have to pay them out of my own vote.

But the treasury would not have to pay the additional amount. We are asked by the different departments to go on voting these increases. It may be said that $3,000, or $4,000, or $5,000, in' one department does not amount to very much, but when you take all the departments the aggregate is a large amount and we find that instead of any effort being made to reduce in some other department, increases are made in different departments, notwithstanding the depression and the declining revenue and the fact that there must be much less necessity for all of these employees than there would be under normal conditions.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
So far as my department is concerned the increase is not very large, and I have given the explanation. We were obliged to employ additional civil servants owing to the added duties developing upon the department. Since the - judgment rendered by the Privy Council on the question of incorporation of companies, the companies formerly incorporated under provincial laws believe that they are obliged to come to Ottawa and be incorporated anew under Dominion laws. It involves additional work and additional expense on the department and we have provided for that new expenditure by an additional sum of $5,000 in contingencies. Generally we ask for new employees, when required, through the Civil Service Commission, according to the law. Whether we obtained these em-

ployees from the Customs or any other department or from outside the service we would have to pay them just the same. The only question we have to consider in this committee is whether this department is in need of them.

Would the minister explain the usefulness of this vote?
Contribution towards publication of International Catalogue of Scientific Literature, $500.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: This catalogue is prepared by an international scientific society which publishes an index of scientific works and this is our share of the expenses. Copies of the index are distributed to the different countries contributing towards its publication and our copies are distributed among the universities in Canada.
What is the total amount contributed by the different nations?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I could not give the total but I know that our contribution is a very small part of the whole amount. We receive nine copies of the publication.

It seems then that we are paying $500 a year and receive nine copies of the catalogue in Canada. I think the minister should .allow the item to stand until he secures some information as to the whereabouts of the society and the proportion of our contribution to the total cost of the catalogue.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: It is published in Brussels. I am willing to allow it to stand. I may say that this item has never been questioned before.

Is it published in only
one language?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: The works are catalogued in the language in which they are published.
Is the minister satisfied that this is a useful expenditure? If he is I have nothing further to say.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Yes, I am.

You take it on trust?
Expenses under the Canada Temperance Act,
Have there been any applications this year by any counties in Canada to have referendums under this Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Yes, many.
This year?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Yes.
How many?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: There -are three pending: one in Brome, one in Perth, and one in Nova Scotia, in Kings county, I believe.
Is this to adopt or revoke the Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
This is for a referendum to the electors under the Canada Temperance Act. If the electors vote for it, the Act will be forcibly applied there. There is a decrease of 518,000 between this and last year's vote. The reason why we had to have $18,000 more last year is that we had to get out lists of the New Ontario constituencies, and of course that will not be necessary this year.
To provide for purchase of 600 copies of the Parliamentary Guide, $1,200.
This is to provide for a new edition of the Parliamentary Guide?

Yes.
Reverend D. R. McDonald, allowance for appropriation of patent ballot, $3,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: This item has to be further considered by the ministers in council, and I would ask that it stand.

I was going to suggest that it should be looked into carefully. I see this is to pay for the patent ballot acquired by the Government some fifteen or more years ago. There is a controversy whether Mr. McDonald really invented the patent or not. I believe that in 1907 he brought a suit in the Exchequer Court against the Government, but it was dismissed. I think the minister should look into it carefully before asking for this vote.

Would the minister give a general explanation of the work of the Printing Bureau, whether there has been an increase or a decrease in the output, whether the facilities have been improved, and such like?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: There is an increase in the salaries paid.
Why?

speechtext: There is more work to do than there was a few years ago, and we have had to employ more men. These employees are in the outside service.
Are these employees in Ottawa, and what class of employees are they?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Yes, they are in Ottawa. They are mechanics mostly.
Do printers rank as outside service employees?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Yes.
Is there an increase in the total number of employees over last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Yes, an increase of about 110 to 120.
How many people are employed in the Printing Bureau?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: About 1,100.
How does that compare with four years ago?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: It is an increase of about 300.
What is the explanation of that increase?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
The output of the Printing Bureau is much greater,
12	noon, and consequently we have had to increase the number of employees. We have been obliged to lease two other buildings.
Where are they situated?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada

One at .the comer of
Murray and Dalhousie street and the other on Sussex street.
Mr. MARCH,: Are these new or old buildings?	.

What is the other?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada

Is all the printing done at the Government Printing Bureau now?

The total expenditure for printing in 1912 was $1,105,000;	1913,
$1,274,000, and 1914, $1,597,000.
What was the cause of this large increase last year as compared with the year before and the year before that?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada

How much of this work was done inside the printing bureau and how much outside?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada

That is more than 25 per cent of the total.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada

Yes, and that is why we asked the House last year for an appropriation for the erection of a new building. We'have not the necessary accommodation to do all the work at the printing bureau.
I have asked again this year for the same appropriation but on account of the stringency it has not been possible to get it. We have not the plant because we have not accommodation.
If the minister is so limited in his accommodation how does he explain the large increase in the number of employees? Where does he find room to put them all?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I have two new buildings. The number of employees has increased but it will be seen from the figures which I have given that the output has also considerably increased.

Is that so? While the total amount of the printing done has increased, the amount done outside is enormously large, over $400,000. speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: The total increase of printing work outside and inside is about $300,000, and the increase in the amount paid for work done outside is about $100,000. The inside output is larger than it was before, there being an increase of about $250,000 a year.

Are these employees kept on during the whole year or are they laid off at certain seasons of the year ?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I have not yet been able to put them out.
The minister has a heavy job before him.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Yes, it is not because I should do it, but it is because we need them all the year round. During the session, when night work is done, we are obliged to take on a few men temporarily. Of course, when the session is over, they have to go. These are the only exceptions.
Is the permanent staff kept on all the year round ?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
The staff is kept at about the same number, because the number taken on temporarily during the session is very small. The work executed by the bureau in 1913-14 amounted to $1,184,185.86, and in 1912-13 to $974,622, so that there was an increase of more than $200,000 for

the last year. In 1913-14 the work done outside amounted to 8412,000, and in 1912-13 to 8300,000. In that case there was an increase of 8112,000.
Are the employees taken from all parts of Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Yes. They do not come under the Act of 1908. We do not have to go to the Civil Service Commission for certificates. They are recommended by those who know them and by the King's Printer. If they prove to be good, they remain in the Bureau. If they are not able to do the work, they have to leave.
Are they mostly printers and binders?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Printers, binders, packers, type-setters, operators on linotype and monotype machines.
Is the political line very closely followed? Is it possible for a Grit, man or woman, to get into the Printing Bureau? Is it an open shop, so to speak?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I believe that the Conservatives are more numerous than they were; but even to-day there is a large number of old hands and new hands belonging to the party of my hon. friend the member for Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil).

I do not think there is a single man or woman from Bonaventure in the Printing Bureau. I am glad to say that the Bonaventure people have healthier work to perform than to be shut up in the Printing Bureau. Is it not a rule of the establishment that no man or woman can get in there unless he is recommended by a member of this House?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: There is no such rule whatever. It is only natural, however, that such should be the case. With one exception, I have never received any recommendations from members on the other side, but I have received recommendations from members on this side.
What happened to that recommendation?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
The hon. member for
Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau) gave a very strong recommendation, and his protege is in the Printing Bureau.
He was successful?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Yes. That is the only such case with which I have had to deal.
Is the Printing Bureau still an open shop or is it a closed corporation so far as trades unions are concerned?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: An open shop. We are obliged to a certain extent to pay the prices established by the unions outside.
Do the rates compare with the Montreal, Winnipeg and Toronto rates?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: The rates paid in the Printing Bureau are based upon the rates paid in Montreal and Toronto.
Are they higher in Montreal than in Toronto?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: The higher rates are paid.

Does the minister expect this year to be able to improve the situation in the bureau by moving to other premises or by enlarging or making a change of any kind, or does he intend during the war to remain where he is now?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I have already claimed that it is impossible to get the necessary appropriation for a new building.
Is there an item in the Estimates for that purpose?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Not this year.
Was there any last year? Air. CODERRE: No.
Then the Government has not decided on anything yet regarding a new printing bureau?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: The principle was decided upon when we came in. I remember having seen a memorandum from the then Alinister to the Council; but last year it was not possible for the same reason that it is impossible this year, that is, on account of stringency.
Has a site been selected for a new bureau?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: No.
Then the question is still an open one?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

Some years ago-I
*forget whether it was before the change of Government or not-there was a good deal of talk about the small pay given particularly to women employed in the printing bureau. The figures given then, in my opinion, were so small that no person would live on them. What is the

average wage paid to women who work in the Printing Bureau?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Two years ago the
wages paid to the women were increased; of course, not very much. The Women had been receiving 75 cents per day for the last 25 years. Two years ago that amount was increased by 25 cents per day. There is another increase. Formerly young girls were paid $3 a week to begin with. We thought that was not enough, and we have been giving them since last year $4 a week as initial salary.

Is not the wage in either case far to small? I cannot conceive of any person, man or woman, being able to live on less than $6 a week in a city like Ottawa. It would be better not to employ those girls at all, than to pay them $3 or $4 a' week.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Some are receiving $8 a week.

I do not think girls can live in anything like respectability and comfort upon $5 or $6 a week if they have to pay for their room and board. What are they to live upon? What is to encourage them in honesty and industry? This is a great country of ours; and when we employ young women and girls to do work for us, we should be willing to pay them respectable wages which will enable them to live comfortably and encourage them to do good work and to live moral and good Christian lives. 'The minister should do one of two things; either not employ those women or girls at all and let them educate themselves to do something outside of Government work, or insist on good quality of labour and pay them well for it.
Legislation-Contingent expenses in connection with the voters' lists, $8,000.
The minister in the past has been supplying members with voters' lists. I suppose the same rule will apply in future.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: We have $8,000 for printing these electoral lists.
Work for the general election has not commenced?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
There is always work
going on in connection with the lists. This $8,000 is for printing lists for by-elections. In some cases members want electoral lists of their counties, and on addressing the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery type-written 
lists are furnished them. As to the printing of the whole lists in the case of a general election, that is provided for by law, and it is not necessary to have a sum in the Estimates for it.
Legislation-Provincial voters' list, $11,000.
What is that?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: That comes under the control of the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery. We have to gather all the provincial lists, as the federal list is based on these lists. The Clerk of the Crown in Chancery receives these lists and pays for them. For instance, in Quebec, so far as the rural part of the province is concerned, the list is prepared every year in September, and we receive these lists.
And you pay the local authorities?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

The lists received by the county clerk in Nova Scotia from the revisors are very often in need of revision, not for the addition of names, but for the correction of clerical errors and so on. I understand that in my own constituency of South Cape Breton, Mr. D. M. Curry, county clerk, received remuneration for this work of revision, which involves extra labour on his part and the employment of more clerical assistants in his office. But for the last two years or more the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery has refused to pay for this extra work. I would like the minister to look into it.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
This is the first time
the matter has been brought to my attention. According to the law, these lists are paid for on the basis of the number of names. The hon. member spoke of corrections, but corrections are supposed to be made by the local authorities. I am under the impression that under the law the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery pays for lists only on that basis of the number of names, and that the lists supplied are supposed to be properly revised. If the hon. gentleman tells me that some other practice has been followed in the past, I am willing to see the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery about the matter.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Having had something
to do with this matter I may say that the lists are paid for at so much per hundred names, and the Clerk of the Peace is bound to under the law to send in the lists re-

vised. The names are counted in the office of the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery and the lists are paid for as the statute provides.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I will attend to that and will see the hon. member about it. Miscellaneous-plant, new, $50,000.
What is this new plant? Mr. CODERRE:	Printing presses, linotype and monotype machines, ruling machines-printing and book-binding plant generally.
What kind of presses does the Government buy?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Meihle presses*
How much of this appropriation for last year was spent?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
The whole amount.
Miscellaneous-miscellaneous printing $100.000.
What is this miscellaneous printing?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
We have to print the
reports of the various departments. 500 of these reports are supplied to the de-part.ment concerned, but in some cases, under Order in Council passed for that purpose, this number is increased sometimes to 2,000 or 3,000 copies. Last year the Department of the Interior, by Order in Council, obtained 7,000 copies.

Does this expenditure
cover the ordinary printing to which the hon. gentleman has referred, or does it cover other printing?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
About nine-tenths of
the amount is expended in the printing of departmental reports. The remainder is for special printing.

Does this vote cover the
general printing of the department, or is it supplementary to another vote? If so, what is meant by miscellaneous printing?

Why do you have this
amount separate from the other big vote which we have just passed?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
This is a special vote
for the general and special reports which I have mentioned.
They are printed by the Printing Bureau?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
It is for the printing
of Departmental reports, either inside or outside the Bureau.
Do I understand that the printing done outside the Bureau is paid for out of this vote?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
If a report is printed
outside, the outsider is paid out of this vote, because, as I have said, this vote covers expenditure for the printing of the reports of departments, general or special.

Whether the work is
done at the Bureau or not?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Whether the work is
done inside or outside the Bureau. I may say that a memorandum respecting the printing of reports has been made by the King's Printer and will be published in the next annual report of the Printing Bureau, which will be ready next week. According to the report of the King's Printer, some departments are receiving too many reports, many of which are lost. The hon. Speaker of the House has given much attention to this matter, as a member of the Printing Committee of the Housp.
Does this $100,000 pay the cost of all the printing that is done by the Government outside the Printing Bureau?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: No. This is a special appropriation for reports printed either inside or outside the Printing Bureau. For other printing done in the ' Bureau, we have a special vote which we call the Auditor General's account. This has already been voted.

I think it would be very valuable information if the minister at some convenient time would lay on the table of the House a statement of the cost of printing for the different departments, of what that printing consists, and the appropriations made for the different items. I was under the impression that the vote for the King's Printer or the Printing Bureau covered all printing, but I find that we are asked to vote under the appropriation for Militia and Defence some $70,000 for printing for the Militia Department. That, I suppose, would be in addition to the vote which the minister has asked for; there may be also other items. I think these items should all be grouped under one heading and the appropriations asked for by the Secretary of State.	I am of opinion that a vast
sum of money is wasted each year in public printing. Large numbers of reports are sent out; many of them are never read. They may make useful additions to libraries and places where they may

be referred to, but many of them are wasted' and thrown away, and many of them are duplicated. Take the Auditor General's Report and the Public Works report ea/ch contains many pages of information which are duplicated in the other. I think that a sub-committee of the Government ought to take up the subject and see whether there could be a very considerable reduction in the cost of printing.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I have given considerable attention to this subject during the present session because of information that was brought to me from time to time that a great deal of this printed matter which was distributed to members was never used by them. Many of them said that individually they did not want the reports and would not use them, ordering them to be taken from their rooms. I then requested the man in the Distribution Office to go to the members individually and procure a written order from each one stating whether he wanted the reports, and if he wanted them whether he would prefer to have them delivered to him here or at his home. In that way we would know what each member wanted and be able to reach a conclusion. But from the information brought to me I am quite convinced that there is an extravagant waste of money in the printing of reports and blue-books. In the first place, there is distribution of more reports to the members than they ever use; in the next place, these reports are duplicated, issued first in blue-book form and then in the sessional paper form and sometimes in some other form. I tried to procure data to place before the Joint Committee on Printing this year in regard to this useless waste of money, but was unable to get all the data I required until late last week, when it was of course too late for the Joint Committee on Printing to go over the data carefully and make an intelligent report to this House. Therefore I was obliged to leave it over. I have now all the necessary data for the consideration of the committee. As the minister has said, the usual number of reports apportioned to a department is 500; but I find that some departments through one request and another, make that up to 3,000 or 4,000. Then through extra orders of this House the distribution to members is sometimes thousands and thousands of copies which are left lying on the hands of the Printing Bureau or of this House and are never used. Ihere are thousands of copies right in this House; they could be taken away in wagon 
loads; no one wants them, and yet they have been printed by an order of this House. It did seem to me that it should be possible to devise some more economical way of printing and to bring about a reduction in the number of reports printed- and distributed to members, many of whom do not want them. I have all the data to be used in future by the committee, and hope to be able to leave it in their possession, so that whenever they come to consider the question with a view to effecting a saving in printing they will have some material on which to work.

I think the House will be thankful to His Honour the Speaker for the trouble he has gone to. He has tackled a long standing grievance that has been a source of expense, annoyance and worry. But if the English-speaking members of this House have reason to complain about the Government literature and printing, what about the poor French member, who gets a double supply? What about his wife at home who receives daily this narcel of blue-books? A member who is in Parliament long enough has either to build an annex to his house to contain ail these blue-books, or burn them as they come in. Has Mr. Speaker given any attention to the printing of blue-books in the French language within a reasonable time? Those of us -who have mixed communities find a very great difficulty in this respect. In my own constituency about one-third of the people are English and two-thirds French. Recently I was asked by two electors for the report of the Auditor General. I sent one copy of the report in English for 1914, three volumes complete. Of the French version. I could send only the first volume of the report for 1913, as the other two volumes for 1913 had not yet been printed. If we are going to issue these official publications in both languages they should be printed within a reasonable time in order to be of any use. Otherwise these French books which come to us a year or two after the date on which they are issued are simply a pure waste of money. When the report of a department reaches the Printing Bureau do they wait until the English edition is printed and bound before starting to print the French edition?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
That is the whole trouble.
I believe that the hon. member is completely in the right when he says it is purely and simply a waste of money if the French publications are not printed and issued within a reasonable time.
They should be issued at least in the same year. I am willing to allow a few months to some of the departments.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
There has been a great improvement in that respect since I took office. The hon. gentleman speaks of the Auditor General's Report, He says that he has received three volumes of the English report for 1914 but only one volume of the French report for 1913, a year old. The other two volumes are just being printed now. By a new arrangement the French version of the Auditor General's Report for 1914 is now being printed, practically at the same time as the English version is printed. I believe that before five months from to-day the French version of the Auditor General's Report for 1914 will be issued.
Mr. MARC1L: If the minister can bring about a reform in that way he is entitled to a great deal of credit, but he has a heavy task before him. I offer my condolences to him beforehand because he will find some of the departments difficult to handle. My idea was that the translation should be made from the manuscript before it is printed. In some cases the translators explained that they had to wait until the bound volume of the English version was issued before starting translation. The objection to translating from the manuscript was that a great many corrections were made on the proofs, after their return, to the departments, and this would naturally increase the difficulties.. I know there are difficulties in the way and if the minister can do anything that will secure publication in French within a reasonable time he will be doing a great service to the country.

The trouble seems to be much more far reaching than has been suggested. I believe the Printing Bureau was established for the purpose of promoting economy and efficiency in the public printing. Before the establishment of the Printing Bureau the printing was all done by private firms under contract and it was said, I believe, to lead to considerable abuse in the matter of patronage. It was hoped that when the Printing Bureau was established this abuse of party patronage and the distribution of printing for the sake of spending money with friends would be done away with, and that the Printing Bureau would give efficiency and economy in the furnishing of the public printing. I have tried to get the facts in connection with the estimate that
I have drawn attention to, but the facts that have been brought out in this discussion show-and it is within the knowledge of every one-that the condition that prevailed before there was a printing bureau at all exists to-day almost to as great an extent as then. So far from the Printing Bureau doing the whole of the Government printing, and thereby promoting efficiency and economy, and cutting out party patronage and expenditure for the sake of patronage, the Printing Bureau is so loaded up with duplicate printing that it is not able to print efficiently or in due time. This is a matter that I think should claim the attention of the Government and of the House. We have a printing bureau for a certain purpose, and that is, to promote efficiency and economy; and we should conduct that bureau so that economy and efficiency would be promoted, and so that we should not be under the necessity of farming out a large proportion of the public printing as a matter of party patronage. For my part, as a printer, I would be perfectly satisfied to see the bureau abolished and the work done under contract by private firms. That might not be the best way; it might not suit the public generally. But I say the work should be done either one way or the other. Either the Printing Bureau should be so organized and so conducted that it would do practically the whole Government printing, or we should cut out this enormous expenditure on the Printing Bureau and get our printing done by contract, just as the ordinary business house does. We have a double disadvantage at the present time.
At one o'clock, the committee took recess.
The committee resumed at three o'clock.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I beg to move that resolution 322:
Reverened D. R. McDonald, allowance for appropriation of patent ballot, $3,000.
be struck out. This is the item that was mentioned this morning. It provides for the payment of $3,000 to the Rev. Mr. McDonald on a claim against the Government for $5,000, his claim being based on his invention of a ballot paper. This item was put in the Estimates on condition that the Commissioner of Patents would give Mr. McDonald a certificate, which he has not done. We were told that the Commissioner of Patents would give him an award of $3,000 for his invention of the ballot now

in use for Dominion purposes. This condition has not been fulfilled, so that we do not believe we should pay the money.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Motion agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
We will now take up
the Department of Mines.
Mr. MARCH.:	Before the minister proceeds to the Department of Mines, I should like to ask him a question concerning naturalization papers. I understand that a certain application was made to his department for blank forms in French and that the reply was that there were no blanks printed in French.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: The naturalization certificate was translated into French about three weeks ago and it will be printed soon. We have to give a temporary certificate in English or French because the real and final certificate has not yet been printed. The form of certificate has been drawn up according to the regulations passed by Order in Council. That form was adopted in English and it has been translated into French. Those who want the certificate form in French may have it but it will only be a temporary certificate.
Whatever form you have will be printed in both languages, I suppose?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

Do I understand
that any person who was a resident of Canada on the 1st January last is still entitled to get a certificate of naturalization as a Canadian citizen? I understand the point was raised in a court of my own province when the judge decided that the effect of the law was that any person who was resident in the country on the 1st January could still get a certificate of naturalization as a Canadian citizen by proving qualifications under the old law.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: This question has been submitted to the Department of Justice. I do not remember the conclusion arrived at by the department but it has been decided that, whatever appears to be the law on that point, these certificates may not be given during the war.

Would the minister be good enough to get the opinion of the Department of Justice and lay it on the table because it is a matter of importance throughout the country that we should know what view they take upon the subject.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I will do that.

What is the procedure
that must be followed by a Canadian who has become an American citizen and who now wishes to return to his original nationality?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I do not know that the the law passed last year has changed that.
Yes, it has.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Well, I could not give a statement as to 'those conditions.

The answer which my hon. friend the minister will get when he receives the opinion of the Department of Justice will be the answer which my *hon. friend from Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil) wants, because the law provides that a person who had given up his allegiance here and had gone abroad could become naturalized again in Canada after a rssi-dence of three months, on taking the necessary oath.
Before the court in the district in which he resides ?

Before the court in the district in which he resides. The question I put to the minister as to the rights of parties under the old law, and the opinion entertained by the Department of Justice as to those people, would settle the question in my hon. friend's case as well as my own. It has been held, I know, that those who may be resident in Canada on- the 1st of January, under a section which came into the Bill after it had passed in this House or which was put in hurriedly at the end, was sufficient to cover residents on the 1st of January of this year.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: When I answered the hon. member a few moments ago I understood his question had reference only to aliens who desired to become British subjects. The question which my hon. friend from Bonaventure asked does not apply to the -same class of foreigners. In the case mentioned by my hon. friend from Pictou, this question has been brought by the Department of Justice to the attention of the Home Government, and it has been decided that, whatever may be the Ipw on that point, aliens coming from foreign countries-not persons who have been British subjects and who wish to return to their allegiance-cannot receive certificates of naturalization during the war. I will bring down all the information I have received from the Minister of Justice.

In view of the changes which have been made in the naturalization law, would it not be possible for the minister to issue a circular giving instructions as to what may be done to enable repatriated Canadians to become British subjects ? The hon. Minister of- the Interior (Mr. Roche) told us last night tha-t the movement for repatriation was still going on in the United States, and that a large number of former Canadians were returning to Canada. Some of these people had become American citizens, and they now want to become British subjects again. Some doubt has arisen as to the naturalization of these persons, and perhaps my hon. friend would take the suggestion in good part that a copy of the certificate might be sent to members of Parliament and others, in view of the approach of a general election. Questions arise as to whether a man has been an American citizen or not, and as to what procedure is necessary in order that he may become a British subject again. In the case that I mentioned, the man was getting ready to vote at the next election, and he wanted to become a fit and proper subject for exercising the franchise. If there has been any change in the Naturalization Act, it will be well to get out circulars and send them to the members of this House and other parties interested so that they may know exactly how the law stands at present.	*

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
We will do that.
Civil Government-Department of Mines ; salaries, $358,775.
Why the increase in salaries?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
There is an increase of six in the number of permanent employees proposed to be employed in 1915-16. The net increase in the amount of salaries over the sum voted for 1914-15 is $12,800, made up as follows: one in second division, subdivision A. This man is already in the employ of the department temporarily. The change has been made according to the custom which has been followed in the Department of Mines for many years. Before making an employee permanent, the department employs a man temporarily so as to give him an opportunity to make good. In this case the man has proved to be competent, and we want him now to be made permanent. He is to hold the position of water analyst at a salary of $1,600. There is a new appointment in third division, subdivision B, a stenographer at $500. We require that stenographer. In the Geological Survey branch there is an appointment in the second division, subdivision
A,	of a junior geologist at $1,600. According to the system followed during the past few years, men selected from the different universities are tried out as temporary employees in the field before being taken on permanently. Three men are now available for employment, and we want one of those three to be made permanent. There is an appointment in the second division, subdivision C, at $1,200. This is required to replace Dr. J. A. Robert, transferred to the well-boring section, Geological division. We want two additional stenographers to replace temporary stenographers in the department. They require special training; and when they prove their ability to do the work, they ought to be appointed permanently. Those are all the new appointments in the Mines branch. We ask for the following promotions in the Mines branch: two from second division, subdivision A, to first division, subdiyision
B,	namely, Mr. H. S. DeSchmid and Mr. E. Stansfield. Mr. Stansfield is engineering chemist at the fuel-testing station, and he is giving eminent satisfaction. He is a thoroughly well-trained man, fitted to engage in original investigation, and his promotion is strongly urged. Mr. DeSchmid is assistant mining engineer in the ore-dressing and metallurgical division. He has compiled a monograph on mica, and he is now working on the felspar and phosphate deposits of Canada. He has had a good training, and is doing very useful work.
That is not exactly what I wanted to get at. Has the Mines branch more work to do than it had last year? If not, what is the reason for increasing the staff?	.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Although it appears that there is more than one increase, there is really but one. Let us take, for instance, the water analyst. He has been employed temporarily for a couple of years, and has never been made permanent. We now think he has proved to be competent and is entitled to a permanent position, and we ask for the necessary money. The same can be said in the case of the junior geologist, although it appears in the Estimates brought down that this is a new appointment. That man has been in the department as temporary employee for seven years. In that way, there is but one increase on the staff, according to the

Estimates brought down, with the exception of the two stenographers we require.

According to page 25 of the Estimates, there were 206 employees in 1914-15, and there will be 212 in 1915-16. That will be 6 of an increase. There is also an increase of $12,800 in salaries. One man would not receive $12,800.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: The hon. member must remember that there are the statutory increases in all those cases. The total increase is $12,800, and the statutory increases amount to $12,212.50. We have no control over the statutory increases.
We must be getting the six new men for practically nothing, because there is only a small difference between the total increase and the statutory increases.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Some men have been replaced by men who are paid less. Although it appears that six appointments have been made, in reality there has been but one new appointment, all the other officials having been temporarily employed for some time.
Who is the new water analyst?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: R. T. Elworthy, who has been temporarily employed since May 14, 1914. He is now employed in an investigation of the mineral waters of Canada in a temporary capacity. This is important work, and will be of long duration. As Mr. Elworthy has proved himself a capable officer, it is proposed to make his appointment a permanent one.

I do not think there is any country in the world that has so much bad drinking water as Canada has. The water we drink here would not be given to cattle in Europe. Does the department provide any supervision of the drinking water which is consumed in large cities, such as Montreal, Toronto and Ottawa?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: No.

Some of the rivers from which drinking water is obtained in this country are half in the United States and half in Canada; some are half in one province and half in another. The water which we drink here 'during the session of Parliament is not fit to drink. Half the Ottawa river is in Ontario, and the other half in Quebec, and I am told that while people are sick in Ottawa they are healthy in Hull. Should not the Dominion

officials exercise some control over this matter?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: We have not that power; in order to obtain it, provision would have to be made to that effect.
On what principle is the examination of mineral waters carried out?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: The jurisdiction of the Department of Mines extends to mineral waters; mines and mineral waters have a certain corelation; and on account of that corelation the investigation of mineral waters comes under the control of that department.
Are these mineral waters to be found in all provinces of Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: In all provinces, yes.
Who was appointed as mining engineer in the fuel testing division?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Edmund G. Malloch, salary $1,600.
Has he all the knowledge required of a person who holds such a position?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Yes, he was appointed upon the certificate of the Civil Service Commission.
I suppose it is the Civil Service Commission that advertises in the Canada Gazette with regard to applications for positions?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: The Civil Service Commission advertises upon request being made by the department for a certain number of employees.

The advertisement in this case struck me as being very peculiar. It runs this way:
Candidates must be graduates in mining engineering of a recognized university, and must possess the following qualifications: a general knowledge of geology, chemistry, and of the mining industries of Canada; particular aptitude for technical statistical work, including accuracy, neatness, and the possession of keen powers of observation and deduction, the ability to prepare clearly and logically written reports; a general knowledge of draughting; a working knowledge of the French language; a pleasing personality.
I find no fault with the minister in this respect, but I do not see why it is required that the holder of this position should have a pleasing personality, provided he is in other respects a capable man, possessing full technical requirements.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: This advertisement was drafted by Dr. Haanel, Director of the Mines Branch. A pleasing personality is really of importance in this position. The mining engineer in the fuel testing division has to meet all the engineers and mining people in the country, and it is better that he should be agreeable and pleasant. Dr. Haanel has had some experience in these matters and I presume that he thought that this was a necessary qualification.
Does the minister not think that $1,600 a year is a small salary for a man possessing those qualifications?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: They start at $1,600, but as soon as they prove competent they pass to subdivision 2 A.
Are mining operations in Canada in a satisfactory condition at the present time? What progress has been made during the last year or two?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: The production generally is not as large as it has been during other years. There are reasons for that decrease, one being the war.

What was the progress
before the war? Was there any increase?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
The increases were in
coal and copper. There was some decrease in gold.
How about nickel?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
I could not give exact
figures, but nickel also' has increased.

A Bill was passed last
year with reference to explosives in mines. Were any appointments made under that law? What was done?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
No appointments were
made. It has been impossible for us to get the money for the buildings necessary for the proper carrying out of the law. Last year I had in the Estimates an appropriation of $63,875 in this connection. The money was not spent and the item appears this year also. But we have not been able to make the progress desired, and when we reach that item it is my intention to propose that it be reduced to $5,000.

This question of explosives in mines has been before the public for some years. We were in hopes last year when the Act was passed that the Government would make the necessary expenditure to carry the provisions of that law into 101
effect. I can understand that this year the Government is trying to keep down expenses, but it does seem to me that there are works that could be better reduced than this. In our own province of Nova Scotia we have very stringent local laws with regard to explosives, but some of the other provinces are not so well protected, and they need such a law as we passed last year to safeguard the miners. If the minister says that nothing can be done this year, I suppose we must accept that; but I would urge him not to overlook it for next year, for the mining people of Canada-I do not speak of mine operators so much as the people who go down into the mines to work-have been looking for years for such protection as this law would give.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
I know that the hon.
member is right. I have been pleading this year, as last year, to get the necessary vote to bring into practical effect the law passed last year. But it has been impossible, for the reasons I have given. I hope that next year we shall be more fortunate. I realize that the situation should be dealt with as soon as possible.

Does the department exercise control over those establishments where explosives are manufactured, as for instance at Rigaud, in Vaudreuil, Beloeil, on the Richelieu river, and other places? Last year explosions took place, with most deplorable loss of life. I have wondered whether the department had any authority over these factories.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: We have authority under the law passed last year, but, as I have explained, we have not the necessary machinery to bring the law into operation, money being too scarce. Without the money necessary to provide the buildings and pay the staff the work cannot go on. Meantime, the situation will have to be dealt with by provincial governments and municipalities under the laws, already provided.
Do the factory laws apply?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
I think they would.
But there are special laws passed by some of the provinces dealing with manufactories of this kind, giving authority to public officers to inspect and in some measure control.

Of course, that to which
I call attention is different from the subject

mentioned by the hon. member for South Cape Breton (Mr. Carroll). He speaks of the use of explosives in mines and I of the manufacture of explosives. Nothing is more [DOT]important than the safeguarding of human life, and if the Department of Mines can do anything to prevent loss of life through these terrible explosions, it would be hard to think of money being better spent. Some of these factories of explosives are right on the line of railway, within half a mile, and there is constant danger to the public. I have never heard whether any action is taken in the case of these explosions, but now is the time for the hon. minister to show what he can do.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: In each of these cases the department has sent one of its principal officials to the scene of the explosion. Of course he could not do much. All he could do was to gather the particulars of the explosion and the extent of injury wrought in the destruction of life and property. He could not do more than that. This is one of the reasons why legislation was introduced by the Government with a view to prevent such accidents. We have not today the necessary machinery to enforce that law, but I hope that next year we will be in a better position.

The question of fuel is becoming a very important one in the large cities. In Montreal there are. some poor people who are buying coal in 25-lb., 50-lb. and 100-lb. lots, while many have to obtain it through charity from the St. Vincent de Paul Society. Coal is selling in small lots at $9, $9.50 and $10 a ton, and by the ton at $8.50. What progress has been made in the introduction of peat fuel? The Montreal Light, Heat and Power Company has introduced a new fuel, coke, which is a byproduct of the manufacture of coal gas and is used by the poor in conjunction with soft coal. It would be of great importance if peat could be introduced as a good fuel.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
For years considerable sums have been spent, not only in Canada but all over the world, in the effort to solve the question of using peat as a fuel. The Government of Canada spent a considerable sum a few years ago at Alfred, in Prescott county, the total expenditure being $25,508. The results, I regret to say, were not satisfactory. That is to say, it has been found impossible to demonstrate by the process followed there that peat could be put on the market at a price which would compare

favourably with that of soft coal. I have since taken much interest in a process owned by a gentleman named Graham in Ottawa. Lately he said that if the department would pay $100 to Mr. Porter, a mining engineer attached to McGill University, for a report he was sure it would be favourable. We have done that, and I have here the report of Mr. Porter. He says:
It is a misfortune that Mr. Graham has been over-sanguine as to certain fundamental matters and it is with sincere regret that I feel myself unable to express unqualified approval of his proposal.
We have been working on that for two years and this is the result. It would be exceedingly important not only during the winter but all the year around if we could put peat on the market at a lower price.
What was the cause of the failure at Alfred, the raw material or the process?	.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Dr. Haanel, Director of the Mines Branch, will not admit that there has been a failure. He claims to have demonstrated that peat could be briquetted at such a price that it could be sold at $3.50 a ton. His report on this question is available to those interested.
Has the manufacture of peat at Alfred been discontinued?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: After the Government experiments ceased, the plant was purchased by a Mr. Shuttleworth, an Englishman, who was deeply interested in the question and who has, since purchasing from the Government, spent through his representative, Mr. Moore, some $50,000 in developing the plant.
Last year I was told that this was a very successful undertaking of Mr. Shuttleworth. How successful has he been this year?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: We are always hopeful in cases like this. I would like very much to have these hopes realized.
Has any progress been made in electric smelting lately?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
In the Supplementary Estimates there is a vote of $10,000 to be spent in the operation of a process for the electric smelting of iron ore named the Motiai-Irving process. The hon. member must have read in the paper last year that a delegation representing iron ore interests, more particularly in the province of On-

tario, came here to meet the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance. They represented that as the ore was of a very low grade it would he well for the Government to give a bounty to the companies interested. Instead of that the Government appointed a commission, composed of three officers of the Department of Mines, to make an investigation; and that commission has made a partial report. If the House passes this $10,000 vote it will be used for the purpose of making experiments with the Moffat-Irving process, which is very well thought of in certain
4 p.m. parts of the country. So far as zinc is concerned I think the sum of $50,000 was appropriated some years ago for the purpose of making experiments at Nelson, but they did not prove a success. These ores are of a very low grade, and a process has not yet been invented for developing them on a paying basis. I beg to move that the amount of $63,875 in the third item of resolution 282 be reduced to $5,000.

What will the minister
do with this $5,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: It is to pay the expenses of the officers who are to make the investigations. Part of it will be used in travelling expenses, and part in making preparations.
If there is an opportunity of enforcing the Act I do not think this item should be cut down.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
It is impossible to get
this money. There is no item for it in the Estimates of the Public Works Department.
The difficulty is that the money does not appear in the Public Works Estimates?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Motion agreed to.
Civil Government-Department of Mines- Mines Branch, second division, subdivision B; 1 at $1,300 ; 1 at $1,275 ; 1 at $1,262.50; 2 at $1,200 ; 1 at $987.50; 1 at $975; 1 at $800, $9,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
I beg to move:
That the said Resolution be amended by adding thereto the words: "including $1,000 transferred for third division, subdivision A, to second division, subdivision B."
This is the same amount as was voted last year for this man. The reason why I ask for the transfer is that when we asked the Civil Service Commissioners for a certi-lOlj
ficate for this man, they told us it would first be necessary to have him transferred.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Motion agreed to. -
Mines and Geological Survey-Mines Branch -investigations of ore deposits, economic minerals, peat bogs, determination of fuel values of coals, lignite and peat of Canada, including wages of machinist and labourers, and additional machinery; investigation of ore dressing, wages of labourers, machinery and equipment of laboratory; collection of information regarding minor minerals, and metallurgical industries and operations, $62,000,

Would the minister give us a sketch of what the intentions are with regard to the expenditure, of the particular objects of the investigations mentioned in the list and in what particular localities it is proposed to make the bulk of the expenditure?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
This is an item of $62,000 for investigations to be carried on by the Mines Branch. The hon. member will notice that there is a decrease of $24,000. The main vote last year for the same purpose was $86,000. This item is to provide for the continuation of investigations into the copper resources of Canada and their utilization. There will be an investigation for the purpose of studying the recent advances and experiments in the hydrometallurgy of copper. These methods are applicable to low grade copper ores which at the present time are not used by our operators. Inquiries have been received with reference to the application of these methods of the recovering of copper to certain Canadian ores. The ore testing laboratories have also been asked to make certain experimental investigations along this line. There is an item of $6,000 for the investigation of iron ore deposits including magneto metric surveys. For the purpose of continuing our investigation of the iron ore resources two field parties are proposed and the areas not yet examined will be surveyed during the field season. The location of the parties cannot be determined until the close of the present field * season, but one party will probably complete the work in Ontario while the other will be sent to British Columbia. There is another item of $2,000 which will be applied to the preparation of a new edition of the report upon the mining and metallurgical industries of Canada. The report is now in course of preparation by Mr. John McLeish, chief of division of Mineral Resources and Statistics. This item of $62,000 is divided into a large number of small items, and I am ready to go on with an

explanation of each of them, but it will take a long time.
I will not press the question; I see that the minister is not prepared to answer it.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I am prepared to go on with the explanation.

It would not really convey the information that I am anxious to have in a way that would he interesting. I wish to make a remark which perhaps is fitting at this place. I want to draw the attention of the minister and his department to the use of the word " lignite " in describing a large part of the coal formation of Alberta and Saskatchewan. A similar class of coal exists south of the line and there a different name is used for it. My information is to the effect that the use of the word " lignite " unduly and improperly prejudices the public mind in regard to the quality of coal so named.
