I may be getting into deep water when I undertake to discuss this question with the scientific members of my hon. friend's staff, but there is no question about the fact that the word " lignite " is properly used as a name for a coal that is not a coal but is a partially formed coal and therefore very inferior as far as burning qualities are concerned.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: What do they call it south of the line?

Sub-bituminous. I would not wish that a name should be used that would convey an impression unduly favourable in regard to the quality of the coal but I am just as insistent that a name should not be used which conveys an idea unduly unfavourable to the quality of the coal.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
What would the hon.
gentleman suggest that we would do in order to change the name?

My suggestion is that a
more appropriate name be used in designating the class of coal that is found in the prairie portions of the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan, a name that would not mark that coal as inferior for fuel purposes when it is not inferior. In the United States they use the term " subbituminous." There is no doubt that this is a more truly expressive term than the term " lignite " which, if I have read the encyclopedia correctly, is applied in its native home to an article that is not yet formed into coal, has not yet the colour of
r Mr. Coderre. 1
coal and has not yet the qualities of coal such as has the coal of the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan. * I am quite aware that this name has been used for many years, but I hope it is never too late to mend.
There is no doubt that great harm has been done by the use of this inappropriate name. Now is as good a time as any to make the suggestion that a more suitable name should be used. The name used south of the line is a much more appropriate and expressive name than the one we use, and might very well be adopted in place of it.
For investigations of the manufacture and storage of explosives in Canada, apparatus and equipment, salaries of inspectors, chemist, machinist, clerical assistance and travelling expenses, $63,875.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I have an amendment before me to reduce the amount to $5,000.
Under what head come the chief reductions in this item?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Under the operation of the law passed last year concerning explosives in Canada, we do not need this money at all, unless we have the money to be provided by the Public Works Department for the erection of the explosives test station and accessories. We cannot get the money from the Public Works Department, and so we do not need this estimate. We have retained $5,000 of it for certain expenses in connection with the operation of the Explosives Act.
For practical tests in road making of tar sands of Athabaska, $5,000.
Is this the second year that this vote has been in?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Yes.
What is it for?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Arrangements were made with the government of Alberta and the city of Edmonton to lay two types of pavement with material obtained from the tar sands deposits of Athabaska river. Mr. Ells, of the Mines branch staff, is selecting the material this summer and is arranging for its transportation in the winter. The tile pavement, the foundation for which will be provided by the city of Edmonton, will be laid some time in the year 1915. There are already 50 tons of that material at Athabaska landing.

The people of Edmonton
and vicinity appreciate very much the action of the minister in taking the course

that he has done in regard to this tar sand. It is a very practical piece of business that he has undertaken, and we hope that the experiment will turn out successfully, as it means a great deal to that part of the country. Has the department decided as to what the form the first experiment will take? There will probably require to be a number of experiments; but if the minister is able to make a statement in regard to what the present intentions of the department are, I shall be very glad to have it.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
It is all experimental
work. This will be the first experiment. A man fully qualified for the work will be sent to Edmonton to represent the department. He will try with all his might to get the desired results. We shall have, moreover, an experienced layer of material at Edmonton for the same purpose.

Will the experiment be
tried out as pavement on the city streets or as improvement of the country roads? When we had this matter under discussion last year, we pressed for an experiment with a view to its application to the country roads. Which experiment is to have the first place in the attention of the department?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: The experiment will be made on the city streets. There is an understanding between the city and the Government in that regard.

That was not the great
purpose that we had in view in bringing . the matter to the attention of the minister at the last regular session. The great purpose was the use of the asphalt in the improvement of the country roads. While, of course, its use in the improvement of the city streets is very good, the great purpose is for the country roads.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
If the experiment proved
useful for the city streets, would it not naturally be useful for the country roads?

It is possible to incur an expenditure in preparation for the laying of the city.streets that would not be practicable in the case of the country roads. We wanted to find out if this would be a measurably cheap as well as efficient improvement for the country roads. Probably fifty tons would not be more than sufficient to try out an experiment thoroughly well on the city streets. Therefore, I would say to the minister that, while I give him every credit for what he has done to solve a practical problem in a practical way.
I still point out that the great purpose of dealing with the country roads will not be altogether served by the means that have already been taken. No doubt it will need a much larger supply of material in order to try out these experiments on country roads, and I should be glad, if during the coming summer, the minister would take that fact into consideration, and secure a still larger supply for the purpose of carrying that experiment further. As to the experiment on the city streets, I do not think there is any question about it, the article is well suited to that purpose. The great problem is to find a cheap means of establishing permanent roads in that country of black soil.

Has the minister had
any analysis made of this so-called black sand deposit in the vicinity of the Peace river? If so, did it indicate the presence of petroleum or of material that would produce gasoline?	*

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: An officer of the department has been working there-Mr. Ells. I am told that he has not yet had time to complete his work, but is gathering the necessary material to make a report. I do not know whether it will be necessary for him, in the meantime, to procure an analysis of that tar sand. I think we shall have to wait until he brings out his report to see if an analysis is necessary.

Far be it from me to assume a knowledge of my hon. friend's department superior to his own, but I wish to inform him that I have already received a very handsome volume containing Mr. Ell's report, upon which I congratulate both Mr. Ells and the department.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I do not remember having seen the report. But what I meant is that Mr. Ells is continuing his work.

Is this asphalt to be
found in quantities sufficient to benefit the whole of Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
The deposit is very
large-millions of tons.

I understand that the
asphalt used in Montreal is all imported. It would be most encouraging to know that material for the making of good roads could be had in our own country. There is much to be done in the way of making good roads in the older provinces.

I understand that the item in regard to explosives has been reduced to $5,000 and passed in that form. But, if I may be permitted, I should like to say a word upon that subject. There are a number of operating coal mines in the constituency I represent, both so-called lignite and actually bituminous coal mines. While fortunately, we have not yet had any serious accident in connection with explosives, I should like to urge that the time to make expenditure for the protection of life against explosion is before the explosion takes place rather than after. As the law has been passed dealing with that subject, which has to be supplemented, by certain expenditures, and as it appears to have been the intention of the Government to provide for those expenditures, I would urge as strongly as I can the reconsideration of the suggestion to cut down that appropriation. There have been very terrible mining explosions from what may be called the natural conditions, but there are < other terrible accidents resulting from the nature of the explosives used. I understand that the legislation that I have referred to provides that proper precautions shall be taken that the explosives shall be in proper order and shall not be tampered with. There is no doubt there was a condition believed to exist which made it necessary to bring forward this legislation; and it seems strange that, the legislation having been agreed to by the House and the necessary expenditure having been considered and considered favourably, the appropriation should now be practically withdrawn. It is not a very large amount, and there is no doubt there are very important interests affected by the expenditure. I merely wished to place before the minister as strongly as I could the conditions as they exist and my views with regard to the matter.
Mines and Geological Survey-Geological Survey branch for explorations and surveys; ethnological, archaeological and palaeontological investigations; wages of explorers, topographers, draftsmen and others, $175,000.

Last year, the hon. minister will remember, I asked for information with respect to the dismissal of Mr. McLeod, who had been in the service of the Government for a great many years. At the time the minister was not able to furnish me with one part of the information asked for, that is, the reason of Mr. McLeod's dismissal. Can the minister give me that information now?	[DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
I remember that
question was put to me, and I had an op-
[Mr. C. Mardl.J
portunity later of going- into the record. The non-employment of Mr. McLeod was not last year, but the year before, last. I was not Minister of Mines at that time, and of course I had to go to the record for the facts. The man has never been a permanent employee; he used to be attached to field parties in Nova Scotia. I cannot find in the record any reason for his not being reengaged for the season of 1913. I believe that a return has been ordered in respect of this matter; I do not remember having laid it on the table, but I do remember having seen it in my office, and if it will give any satisfaction to my hon. friend I shall be glad to look for it, and bring it down Monday or Tuesday.
Who has been appointed in Mr. McLeod's place?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: He was only a temporary employee, working during the few months of the year in which these field parties were engaged. If he has been replaced, I do not know by whom.

I am not surprised that the hon. minister is unable to give, any reason for Mr. McLeod's dismissal. The fact is that there was no reason for his dismissal, unless it was that he was one of my supporters. Mr. McLeod-this will show how little he was interested in politics-did not go home to vote at the last election. He had been in the service of the Government for twefiiy-five years, and had been efficient in his work, a fact which I feel sure the Government has utterly failed to recognize. It is absurd to dispense with the services of a man who has worked faithfully for twenty-five or thirty years. The minister says that a report was asked for. I got that report last year, and I was glad to know that all the officers employed in the Geological Sur-very spoke of Mr. McLeod as a most efficient man, whose services could not very well be dispensed with. I have a clear recollection of a favourable statement made by Mr. Fletcher, who was the head of the department while he lived; in his death the country suffered a great loss. In view of Mr. Fletcher's favourable recommendation of this faithful servant of the Government, and in view of the fact that the Government could not charge Mr. McLeod with active political partisanship, it is not surprising to me that the minister is unable to give any reason for his dismissal. I may suggest a reason, however : on account of personal animosity

between Mr. McLeod and some of the politicians in the counties of Inverness and Victoria, Mr. McLeod was victimized. If the facts were laid before the committee, hon. gentlemen would realize that Mr. McLeod's services were dispensed with because some of these politicians got itfhe ear ox my hon. friend's predecessor. I -am sure that my hon. friend's predecessor did not know the facts, or he certainly would not have dismissed Mr. McLeod. Last year I suggested to the minister that he should look into this case, and, if he found the facts to be as I represented them to him, that he should, on behalf of the Government and his department, offer to reinstate Mr. McLeod in the position, that he might continue to do the good work which he had been doing for so many years. What encouragement is there for any persons in the 'service of the Government to do honest work if they must look forward to the time when they will be thrown to the dogs, so to speak, at the instance of those who have not the slightest desire to further the interests of the country or to assist in the efficient administration of the department ? Persons of this kind care for nothing but the satisfaction of their own desires. I hope the minister will take this case up, and offer Mr. McLeod the position that he held for so many years. It is no explanation to say that he was only temporarily employed, because the work which he did could only be performed during six or seven months of the year. My hon. friend must remember, however, that this service was continued for 25 years or 30 years. Mr. McLeod worked during the summer, and istayed at home in the winter, doing clerical work for the department. I do not know whether Mr. McLeod would undertake the work again, but I think if would be a good thing if the minister would take the matter in hand and teach a lesson to those person's who have interfered.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
As I have already said, I do not know why Mr. McLeod was not rq-engagedi in 1913; neither do I know whether I can find out. In the return which has been mentioned, there is a recommendation of Mr. McLeod by Mr. Fletcher. I am told that Mjr. McLeod was not employed continuously for 25 years. On one occasion the hon. member for Edmonton did not re-engage him; for what reason, I do not know. If my predecessor refused to re-engage Mr. McLeod because of partisanship, how am I to ascertain -whether he was right in the course which
he took? I will inquire into the matter, but if if is proved that Mr. McLeod has been guilty of political partisanship, I do not think my hon. friend will insist upon my taking him back.

I certainly will not. Mr. McLeod's 'suspension at the time referred to by the hon. minister was due to little domestic troubles which he had with my hon. friend's predecessor; it was not on account of partisanship. I am sure that my hon. friend would not look unfavourably upon Mr. McLeod for anything he had done against my hon. friend's predecessor. If Mr. McLeod was not re-employed because of non-partisanship or because of his not taking a sufficiently active part in politics, it is evident that he is going to be damned if he does take part in politics, and he is going to be damned if he does not. It is not safe for him to go into politics, and it is not safe for him to keep out of politics. The hon. minister certainly can make no charge of political partisanship against Mr. McLeod, and I am sure that he can find nothing else against him. I am encouraged to think, therefore, that the minister will take into consideration the 'suggestions which I have made in this matter.
Does the vote cover explorations for economic minerals5'

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: These field parties will cover the country and collect data during the summer which will be used in the reports for the year, giving all the particulars of the country examined, the nature of the soil, the geological formations and the general character of the country. People will then be able to judge from these reports whether minerals will likely be found in certain localities. I do not mean that we will go prospecting or engage in the exploitation of mines. This year we will have parties working in Queens-Shelbume, N.S., examining the gold-bearing areas and will also carry on further investigations in connection with the coal measures. In New Brunswick there will be five field parties at work.
What are the parties looking for in New Brunswick?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
They will investigate
general geology in some districts, and make special investigations of the oil shales. In Quebec there will be five field parties, the principal investigations there being in connection with asbestos, mica and graphite.
What are the areas and purposes of exploration in the prairie provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: In Manitoba there will be an investigation of the gold and copper deposits at Beaver lake and general geological work. In Saskatchewan and the Northwest territories there will be special examinations of the Devonian area of the Great Slave lake district, with special reference to the occurrence of oil, lead and zinc. In Alberta there will be further examination of the coal measures and an investigation of the occurrence of underground supplies of water in the neighbourhood of Lethbridge.

There is at present a somewhat pronounced rush from Edmonton to some point on lake Athabaska to an alleged find of silver, in fact of cobalt. Has that particular area been the subject of examination by the geological survey and have steps been taken by the minister to have an examination of this district during the coming summer. I believe it is at the eastern side of lake Athabaska, in the neighbourhood of Pond du Lac.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: No special investigation has taken place in this district. In view of what has taken place recently, we shall endeavour to ascertain if there is any foundation for the reports of discoveries and if there is we shall have an examination made. We have nothing in the department on which to base an opinion as to the value of the alleged discoveries.

A certain prospector has been operating in that territory for two or three years. During the past winter, after the ice set, he came out and brought with him a number of samples. I did not see the samples, but I heard at the time about them being brought out. About two weeks ago there was published in the newspapers quite a startling report as to the assay value of these samples, and on the strength of that report quite a number of prospecting parties have started from Edmonton for the purpose of locating claims. If the department would take steps to see the samples this man brought out, they could satisfy themselves as to the merit of the strike. I have no knowledge myself of the actual value of the samples, but as a number of parties of men have outfitted at great expense for the purpose of going down there, I think it would be quite in order for the department to send out an expert to look over the field to see what merit there might be in it. The place is easily accessible in

summer time. I think this would be a wise step on the part of the department.
Is there anything new in the shale industry in New Brunswick?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I can perhaps tell my hon. friend about that. A friend of his in the Senate, Col. Domville, is very deeply interested in the shale business in New Brunswick, and I think some members of this House too. A little before war broke out, arrangements had been made under which a large amount of English capital was coming in for the development of that industry, but the war has prevented that for a time.

Is it in Westmorland
county?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
No, Albert county chiefly. The matter is now being taken up again, and I understood from Col. Domville the other day that a diamond borer belonging to the local Government had been placed at their disposal, and that further explorations were being made. There are several different shale propositions in the county of Albert. I think Sir William Mackenzie is interested in one of the companies, but not much has been done on account of the war. The general impression is that there is very great wealth in the shale there. The shale will be reduced to oil, and will give very many valuable by-products. The shale has been tested in Scotland at the shale works at Pumperston, and has been found to be as rich as the best shale. The shale question has been talked of in New Brunswick for a great many years, and a good deal has been done. Different companies have been formed, but the difficulty has always been that a very large amount of capital is required in order to place the business on a proper basis. I was talking two or three years ago to Dr. F. S. Pearson, of New York, whom my hon. friend may remember as a scientist and a company promoter. He is the gentleman who promoted the Dominion Coal Company. He told me he was satisfied that in the near future there would be established in the county of Albert an industry that in dimensions and importance would be much greater than the Dominion Coal Company.
The delays have been somewhat
5 p.m. disappointing to the people of
New Brunswick, for everybody in that section is extremely anxious that something should be done to develop this mineral wealth, which is universally believed to be of very great importance.
What is this oil used for?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
For fuel chiefly, for the
use of engines, steamships, and things like that.
And for lighting purposes?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I do not think so. It is
very rich in sulphate of ammonia, which enters very largely into the composition of fertilizers. Then there are all sorts of byproducts from which aniline dyes and things of that sort are made.

I think the industry is
an important one in every respect.
Mines and Geological Survey-Geological Survey Branch-for exploration and investigating the possible occurrence of radium bearing ores in Canada, and for the dissemination of information concerning these ores, $10,000.

Has anything been done
about this?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: There have been no results as yet.

Are these finds expected
to be made in the West?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I do not see that anything has been done so far. We have a tentative programme of field work for this season.

I might say that this particular item goes entirely beyond and is entirely different from the intention of the preceding item. My hon. friend pointed out that the preceding item was not for the purpose of actually prospecting. This particular item is for the purpose of prospecting.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: For exploration and investigation.

Yes, it is for the purpose of prospecting. I am not finding fault with that at all. I think it is a very proper purpose in which to spend a small amount of public money and employ the talents of the officers of the department. But what I wish to urge is that the same attitude be adopted by the department with regard to other minerals that might be found from time to time. I would suggest that a specialty be made of prospecting for particular minerals.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Owing to the interest being taken in radium, and owing to the fact that radium-bearing minerals are for the most part unknown to the ordinary
prospector, the department thought fit to do this exploration themselves.
I am supporting the department in that.
Who has succeeded Mr. Fletcher as chief of the exploration work in Nova Scotia?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Dr. Hayes. There will be several field parties in Nova Scotia this season.
There is a Dr. Hayes who is the provincial Tory organizer and a friend of my hon. friend from North Cape Breton. I suppose this is a different man?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

Perhaps my hon. friend will give some statement as to his experiences and qualifications, with particular reference to coal.
Mr. CODERR.E: His full name is Albert Orion Hayes. He was employed as an assistant to Charles Camsell, Geological Survey, season 1907, at $75 per month; assistant to W. H. Boyd, seasons 1908-9; assistant to R. G. McConnell, seasons 1909-10-11; chief officer in charge of party, May 14,	1913. Appointed to
position of junior geologist in subdivision A of the second division in the Geological Survey, at $1,600 per year, from 9th November, 1914, per Civil Service certificate dated 9th November, 1914. He will be at the head of a party which will operate in Nova Scotia during the coming season to make an investigation of the coal measures at New Glasgow.

Dr. Fletcher was a man who had a wonderful reputation among all the coal people in the province of Nova Scotia, and, now that he is gone, that fact may not have any significance or importance. But I would like to point out that Nova Scotia is the only coal-bearing province, with the exception of a small quantity that is found in New BrunswicK, east of the Rocky mountains.
What?
With the exception of Alberta.
East of the Great Lakes.

East of the Great Lakes, as my hon. friend (Mr. Sinclair) says, would probably be more accurate. There was a great deal of Dr. Fletcher's work which was not complete. There is

quite a problem, as to which he entertained a strong opinion, as to whether coal exists north of the conglomerate formation. He was of the opinion that there existed a very large bed of coal extending from the conglomerate formation down to the coal fields of Cumberland county. He was making an investigation into that question when he was called away. The coal area of Nova Scotia is limited to Pictou and Cumberland counties on the mainland of the province. Of course, Cape Breton Island is by itself. It is a matter of very great importance that the particular phase of the subject to which I have referred should be investigated. I hope that Dr. Hayes, who is the successor of Dr. Fletcher, will have his attention called to that fact. I notice the statement that he is exploring in the vicinity [DOT] of New Glasgow, but that is somewhat to the eastward of the point 1 mentioned.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Not very far.

No, not very far. It is in the present coalfield, which is delimited by the conglomerate foundation. The question is as to the existence of coal between the conglomerate and the coal measures of Cumberland. As to the existence of coal there in large quantities, Dr. Fletcher had very pronounced views. I would like to ask the minister to take a note of this fact, with the view of directing the attention of Dr. Hayes, who, I hope, will prove a worthy successor to Dr. Fletcher, to the possibility of developing that field in the province of Nova Scotia. The coal fields of Nova Scotia being limited, in the mainland of the province as distinguished from Cape Breton, it is most desirable that the idea of Dr. Fletcher should be followed up, in order to make sure of the existence of what he believed to be a large bed of coal. It would add to the coal resources of the country, 'and it would be a very great and important work if the department should locate, at a depth where they could easily be worked, coal measures as to the existence of which Dr. Fletcher was quite confident.
Mines and Geological Survey

Geological Survey Branch-for publication of reports, translation of reports into French, maps, plans, illustrations, etc., $75,000.
I have not seen any reports from the Geological Survey of late with reference to the province of Nova Scotia, although I have noticed pamphlets relating to other portions of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I do not remember having seen a report of the work done in Nova Scotia, but I will ascertain if tnere is one.
I think we ought to have a report on that work soon.

May I ask as to the time elapsing between the geological exploration and the publication of the report of the exploration? In times gone by there seemed to be such an interval between the exploration and the publication of the report that the value of the exploration in many cases was largely lost. I would like to know if anything has been d6ne under the present minister to speed up the production of reports. In regard to the Ells report, I think it is entirely creditable to Mr. Ells, to the department and to the printing shop that did the work. I would like to see that illustrious example followed in regard to everything else.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Last year the Deputy Minister of Mines drew my attention to the delay. As my hon. friend has said, that delay in almost all these cases is fatal. Some of these reports were useless when they were printed, published and distributed. To obviate that inconvenience we thought it would be better to have these reports printed by one firm because it was impossible to print everything at the Printing Bureau. Having to send something outside, and believing that these reports should be as well printed as possible, we have made a contract with the Mortimer Company, Limited, of Ottawa. I believe that, as a result, the reports will present more uniformity, will be brought before the public sooner, and will be printed in such a manner that they can be sent out of the country without the Government or the people being obliged to gloss them over. They will compare favourably with reports of the same kind, the world over.

It is not only a question
of printing the reports; it is a matter of compiling them. Can the minister say that the reports of the explorations that will be made during the coming summer will be available for the use of the public by the succeeding spring? The explorations having ceased at the end of summer, the explorers should make their compilations and the printers should do their work before the following spring, so that those who are interested in following up for economic purposes the information secured would

have that information available in time for its use in the following spring. That is the purpose that should be aimed at.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: The report of the work done last year will come out within a month, and the report of the work done during the coming season will come out very early next spring. It is impossible to bring them out with more rapidity than that.

Without being too insistent, let me urge upon the minister that prospecting work begins as soon as spring begins. The prospector, if he is going into a distant part of the country, requires the whole season to make an effective summer's work; and if the information that has been secured by the Government through its officers in the Geological Department is available during the month of March, then he has the whole summer in which to do his work based upon that information; but if that report is not out before June, then he has only half the summer and can do only half as effective work in the interest of exploration and development.
Therefore, permit me to insist that the minister and his department should use every endeavour to have the results of the explorations of the coming year available before the beginning of the season of exploration in the following year.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada

speechtext:
I am very glad to hear that. Between the minister and myself,
I am very glad to compromise on April.
To what extent does the department exercise supervision over the operation of coal mines upon lands leased from the Dominion Government ?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I do not know anything .about that. That matter belongs to the Department of the Interior.

The minister does not nnderstand me. He is head of the Department of Mines, and anything relating to that department would centre in him. A person obtains a coal lease in Alberta, and proceeds to operate a coal mine. I am not speaking about the payment of rent or .anything of that kind; I am speaking about the operating of the coal mine. Does the Department of Mines exercise any supervision or make any regulations as to the precautions that must be taken by the operator, or what is the line of demarcation between the control of the Federal Government and the control of the Provincial Government ? Those lands being the property of the Federal Government, and in that respect conditions being different from conditions in the East, where the coal area is the property of the Provincial Government, it would occut to me that some duty would be cast upon the Federal Government in ^regard to the operation of the mine. Take the question of safety of life. Where the Provincial Government owns the land and gives it to the operator for a consideration, the Provincial Government lays down certain laws in regard to the manner in which the mine shall be operated, in regard to the safety of the lives of the workmen, and so on. Does this Government do that in regard to any of its properties ?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Those regulations do
not belong to this department at all. I do not know whether they exist or not; but, if they do, they must have been passed by the Department of the Interior.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
If my hon.
friend will allow me, something passed under my notice within the last week or two with reference to this matter. Those lands are leased by the Department of the Interior. The correspondence which passed under my notice stated that they seemed to have been leased by the Interior Department up to the present time; that those who worked them, worked them just as they wished without any supervision as to the manner of taking out the coal, the mining of the coal economically and without regard to the future. That was the representation from .a very influential quarter, urging that there should be supervision. That matter is before the Prime Minister and the Minister of the Interior. I thought that plea was a very

proper one, as it was very uneconomical to have those mines worked without a proper system and a governmental supervision. Therefore that matter will be taken into consideration.

In the province of
Nova Scotia, which has been a mining province for a long period, although a lessee is operating a mine he cannot proceed to take out the coal as he pleases. He must mine in a certain way; he must file plans with the Government, and the Government inspectors can prevent him from taking coal out of a certain pillar or from removing certain protections for the future. Are there any provincial laws on the subject?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I should judge, from the correspondence which passed through my hands, that the matter would belong to the Dominion Government, it being the lessor of the land.

A great many men from my province are working in those coal mines. There have been quite a number of disasters of late, and it has been a subject of discussion amongst the friends of these men in the east as to where the responsibility rests, and as to the wisdom of exercising some control over the method of mining, which is important in the interest of life as well as of property.
Grant to Canadian Peat Society, $1,500.

Is the department still
making experiments with peat?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
No, we are not making experiments. This is a grant to the society.
Civil Service Commission, salaries, $32,037.50.

Is there any provision
here for the appointment of a third commissioner?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: No.

No intention of making
such an appointment this year?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
I could not say as to
that.
Is the salary provided by statute?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
I think it is, but I am not sure.
Department of Naval Service-to provide for the maintenance and upkeep of ships, Naval College and dockyards at Halifax and Esquimau, and Royal Naval Canadian Volunteer Reserve, $1,000,000.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: We should like some explanation of this from the minister.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. D. HAZEN (Minister of Marine and Fisheries) :
speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: On Monday morning, on the second reading of the Bill for granting aid to His Majesty for military and: naval defence, I will make a statement in regard to the working of the Naval Department in connection with the present war; and so I will not refer to it now. This is an amount appropriated for the Naval Service, the same as in the Estimates of last year. It is doubtful whether any large portion of this vote will be expended. The expense of carrying on our naval end of the war, with the Niobe, the Rainbow, the submarine and other ships engaged in the Naval Service and placed at the disposal of the Admiralty, are being paid out of the war vote. I thought at first I might cut down this vote very materially; but in discussing the matter with the Finance Department, it was pointed out that this would not be a safe policy, for if the war came to a sudden termination, we must have some vote on which to fall back to carry on the services, which could not then be charged up to the war appropriation.
Is the cost of operating the Niobe and the Rainbow not paid out of the civil vote?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No, out of the war appropriation.

There is no authority
for that, surely.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Our information is that
there is ample authority under the war vote.
Of course, you can read anything you want to in that war vote. However, I will not discuss that now.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It may be that only a small portion of this $1,000,000 will be required during the war. I will read how it is made up: Royal Naval College, $90,000; dockyard at Halifax, $200,000; dockyard at Esquimalt, $85,000; for the Royal Naval Canadian Volunteer reserves, $200,000; salaries at headquarters and other miscellaneous expenditures, $50,000; amount available for His Majesty's Canadian ships Niobe and Rainbow and submarines CC-1 and CC-2, $375,000. Total, $1,000,000. The amount for the Royal Naval College at Halifax will have to be expended. Some of the other amounts will have to be expended, but if the war continues, a comparatively large portion of it, I hope, will not !be expended.
What doe3 it cost to operate the Niobe and the Rainbow?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The estimated cost of operating the Niobe for the year-^this is based on the expenditure during the present war -is $726,125, and the Rainbow, $366,450. For operating the two submarines, $170,075; submarine depot, $38,800; Halifax dockyard, $257,500; Esquimalt dockyard, $173,350; Royal Naval College, $90,000; the Shearwater, which is the name of the Esquimalt dockyard, $207,425; Atlantic defences, $296,000; Pacific defences, $229,500.
In this vote is not included the amount requisite for the operation of the ISftobe and the Rainbow?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: During the war, no.
Supposing there were no war?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: These boats, when war broke out, were placed at the disposal of the Admiralty. When the war is over the expense of operating these ships cannot any longer be charged up to the war vote, and it is necessary, in case the war comes to a sudden termination, to have a vote from which these expenses can be paid. As I said before, my impression had been that it would not be necessary to have .such a large amount as $1,000,000, the amount which was voted last year, but after considering the matter the Deputy Minister of Finance thought that if this amount were not provided difficulties might arise if the war came to a sudden termination.

Of course, it is a very nice problem to determine what amount should'be expended from the ordinary sums voted by Parliament for the maintenance of any service directly involved in the war, and what should be taken from the credit vote of $50,000,000. This is a matter to which I think the Government have not given very careful attention. It is true that they insist upon passing Orders in Council for every expenditure made under the war credit vote, but I want to submit to the minister that in the ordinary vote there is a certain amount for the maintenance and operation of the Niobe, and that amount could be used, notwithstanding the fact that the Niobe is now under the control of the Admiralty and engaged in war operations. Supposing we were not in a state of war. The Niobe is in our possession and in any event it would cost something to operate her, for which purpose there
is a vote in our ordinary Estimates. This amount might be used, as far as it will go, towards the cost of operation at the present time. I think the same thing is being done in England. They have experienced some difficulty in working it out so as to adjust properly the expenditure which comes from the war credit vote and that which comes from their ordinary supply. I doubt very much whether it can be said that the vote made by Parliament for the maintenance of the Canadian nayal ships should not be applied in some way; the expenditure should not, at any rate, be all charged to the war vote.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That view presented itself, and was considered. The opinion entertained by officers of the department was ' that it would be most difficult to adjust it in the way suggested by my hon. friend. As a matter of fact, I recollect that one of the officers of the department told me that it had been found practically impossible in the case of the British navy to work out a system of that kind. As the money is paid by the country in any case, the matter would not seem to be of very great importance.

I notice that the vote
includes an appropriation for the Royal Naval Canadian Volunteer Reserve. Will the minister tell us if he is making any progress in regard to obtaining volunteers for the navy, and what action he has taken in the matter generally?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
We commenced organizing naval volunteers in British Columbia, where there was already a volunteer organization. Although no provision _ has been made by the Government for it, even before the regulation referred to by the hon. member for Guysborough was parsed a large number of citizens had organized at their own expense in Victoria and Esquimalt a naval volunteer reserve force. All we had done up to that time to assist them was to place at their disposal a shed and other facilities for their training at Esquimalt. We proceeded to organize a naval volunteer reserve there, and they have been a very useful body. We have been absolutely prevented from proceeding further with the work by reason of the fact that it has been impossible to get competent instructors to take charge of these naval volunteers. The naval reservists who were in this country before the war broke out have since joined the British

navy, and it has been difficult to get competent men to act as instructors. The organization in Victoria, however, has proved to be of great value. A large number of the men have gone on board the Rainbow, and many have been there ever since. Numbers of the men are serving in different capacities, as follows: on the Rainbow, 57; on the Aid, a ship engaged in connection with naval work, 20; on the Prince George, which was chartered for a time as a hospital ship, 18; in the barracks on shore duty, l76; in other capacities, about 107. This makes 35 officers and 387 men, a total of 422.
Have these men enlisted for any stated number of years?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: They have enlisted for the duration of the war, or for three years; that is to say, the length of service is three years, and if the war lasts that long, at the end of the three years their contract has been completed and they are at liberty to retire from the service.
They are not all on the Rainbow?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Some are on the Rainbow, some on the Prince George, and some on the Aid.
Are there none on the Niobe?

The minister
might give us the enlistment strength of the Niobe.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
On the Niobe there are about 700 and on'the Rainbow about 300 The Niobe was manned by a certain number of men when the war broke out. On the Pacific coast there were two small British vessels, the Shearwater and the Algerine, which were the last remnant of the British navy on the Pacific coast. Those boats were kept at Esquimalt. They were small vessels of about 1,000 tons each and were used for the purpose of flying the British flag where it was thought well to do so. At the time the war broke out both of these boats were in Mexican waters to show the British flag there. They came up along the coast and, as a matter of fact, day in and day out, we were watching for signs of them because there was very great fear that they would be captured by German cruisers which were understood to be abroad in the Pacific ocean. These vessels made their way up to Esquimalt again and they never sighted the Germans. One of

them, in fact did not know that war had been declared until she arrived at Esquimalt. They are very slow boats making about ten knots an hour. The British Government laid these two boats up at Esquimalt. They gave us one of them as a parent boat to the submarines and the crews of the two boats were brought across and placed upon the Niobe at Halifax. In addition to that we enlisted several hundred naval reservists, thoroughly trained men, with experience in the British navy and still young enough to serve, in the city of Toronto, and in addition to that we have about 100 naval reservists from Newfoundland.
How many came from the two ships of the British navy?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I think not quite 300.
Did Captain Corbett come from one of them?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
He was captain of the Algerine and he took command of the Niobe.
Sir WILFRID LAL'RIER: Will the statement which my hon. friend promised for Monday contain a full statement of the ships of which our fleet is now composed?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes, all the ships we have and the number of men in the service. I shall also state what part we have taken since the war broke out.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Could my hon. friend give us to-day information about the naval college?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
We have in the Royal
Naval College 28 cadets. The number applying for the examinations in the month of April this year show that our accommodation there, which is only about 45 students, will be taxed to the utmost for the first time. As the college continues and the work it is doing becomes appreciated the number of applications is increasing.
What is the age at which young men are admitted?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Between 14 and 16; not
over 16. We have had to refuse applications in a good many cases where young men were over 16 years of age. Some of the oases seem hard but we must not depart from the rule because if these young men are to have a career in the navy they must enter under 16 years. A man entering the college at 16 would be handicapped because when he joined a ship he would be older than the other midshipmen and it would not be

satisfactory from any standpoint. The age in England is between 13 and 14 years. In Canada the limit was fixed at 16 because it was thought, and properly thought, that our boys are not allowed to go away from home to school as early as they are in England.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I would like a statement of the organization of the college, the number of professeors, etc.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The captain in charge, who is the head of the college, is Captain E. H. Martin. He is not on salary as a professoT, but is on the list of the Halifax dockyards. The director of studies is Mr. B. F. Hartley; the naval instructor, Mr. C. G. Allin; the engineer lieutenant, Mr. Angus D. M. Curry. There is also a boatswain, Mr. G. W. Brooker, who does practical work in connection with the instruction of the cadets. The civillian masters are Messrs. L. N. Richardson, John D. Pinhey, and A. C. Hatcher. In addition there is a matron of sick quarters, Mrs. F. L. Barnstead. The subjects taught at the college are mathematics, navigation, mechanics, physics, chemistry, engineering, seamanship, pilotage, either French or German, English, geography and history, including naval history. After serving with the college for some time these young men go to sea, where they are taught seamanship, pilotage, gunnery, torpedo-, applied electricity, mathematics, navigation, engineering, applied mechanics, ship 'construction, and the principles of heat and steam. At the end of each college term the progress of the cadets is tested by examination. We have at present serving on the cruiser Berwick eight cadets under Naval Instructor David A. F. Robinson. These cadets are William J. R. Beech, Thos. S. Critchley, John C. I. Edwards, Donald St. Geo. Lindsay, Howard E. Reed, Henry W. Soulsby, Cuthbert R. H. Taylor, Robert W. Wood. Among those who are serving in His Majesty's Navy in this fight are a number of college cadets, and from the reports we have received they have covered themselves with credit. One of them is a son of my hon. friend from Temiscouata (Mr. Gauvreau), and we have received very good reports about him. My hon. friend was good enough to send me a photograph of his son in uniform, and I am sure there could not be a finer looking specimen of Canadian manhood. Four of our cadets were lost in the disaster to the Good Hope: G. V. W. Hatheway of Fredericton; M.
Camm of Yarmouth; and A. W. Silver and W. A. Palmer, both of Halifax.

They were all cadets
from the Halifax college?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.
The minister has given us the names of those serving on the Berwick. On what ships are the other cadets from the college?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: They are serving on different ships. The names of the Canadian officers serving on His Majesty's ships are: Charles T. Beard, sub-lieutenant; Victor G. Brodeur, sub-lieutenant; Geo. P. Clark, engineer lieutenant; Stanley N. DeQuette-ville, engineer lieutenant; L. J. M. Gauvreau, midshipman; Frank H. Jefferson, engineer lieutenant; Hubert J. Napier Hemy, engineer lieutenant; Percy W. Nelles, lieutenant; John Eric W. Oland, midshipman; John M. Grant, midshipman; and Geo. C. Jones, midshipman. The father of Charles T. Beard is a civil servant, I believe, here in Ottawa. Victor G. Brodeur is a son of Mr. Justice Brodeur of the Supreme Court, and L. J. M. Gauvreau is a son of the-hon. member for Temiscouata.
On what vessels are Midshipmen Murray and Dand?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: They are both serving on the Niobe.
What other midshipmen are on the Niobe?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: R. I. Agnew, L. W. Murray, D. B. Moffat, G. A. Worth, J. D. Laurie, H. R. Tingley, A. F. L. Wilkinson, Alex. H. Dand, Ronald C. WTatson.
How many cadets altogether are serving in the navy?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
About twenty, besides the eight cadets serving on the Berwick. I do not know whether my hon. friend from Pictou was in the House when I was saying that we believe the college will be crowded to full capacity after the April examinations. The college is situated in the naval yard at Halifax, in what used to be the hospital building. If the college continues to grow as we expect, it will be necessary in the near future to seek better quarters. It occurred to me when I was in Halifax last summer that a magnificent site for a naval college would be that splendid property in Halifax where the Admiral used to live. The house is magnificent, but I do not know whether it would be suitable

for a college, and the grounds are very beautiful and extensive.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: As far as I can judge, the organization of the college seems to be very thorough. I hope my hon. friend will be able to bring it up to the standard of the Royal Military College at Kingston, which is a great credit to Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I quite agree with my hon. friend that the military college is a great credit to this country, and that standard will be something for us to keep in view. The military college at Kingston turns out young men capable of filling positions not only in military but in civil life. We hope to make the naval college as great a credit to the country as the military college at Kingston.
When was the organization of the naval college commenced?

I would like to ask the hon. the Minister of Naval Affairs (Mr. Hazen) what are the disbursements per month in connection with the operation
of the Niobe, exclusive of the wages that are paid to the officers and men?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: For stores and provisions on the Niobe the expenditure was $96,675. The total expenditure for stores of all sorts, including provisions, clothing' allowance, medical stores, naval stores, stationery, freight on stores, dockyard stores and contingencies, is $305,575.	.
What is the $98,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service

IMr. Hazen.]
How does the minister purchase the provisions?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service

The following letter is addressed to the editor of the Union Advocate of Newcastle:
Dear Sir,-We would like to know from the authorities at Ottawa how it is that the manager ot the wireless station here is an American who persists in displaying the American flag over his office door, so that all Britishers and others entering must pass under it; also that all Canadian and British employees have been discharged and a number of foreigners taken on instead. Is the Universal Radio Syndicate an English company, or is it an alien company? If the latter, why the need for a guard?
(Sgd.) Subscriber.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: What is the name of the paper?
The Union Advocate, of Newcastle, N.B., where the wireless system is established.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: Has it any circulation?
Yes, it has some circulation.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes, it is an old paper; I have known it for a long time. It used to be published by Mr. Amslow years ago.

It is pot published or
owned by Mr. Amslow now. It is a dyed-in-the-wool party paper. I suppose I can answer the question of the writer insofar as to say that the Universal Radio Syndicate is an English company. Still I am sure it would be interesting to the public at large to know the circumstances under which this wireless system was taken over by the Government. It was constructed very recently, and it was not much more than in working order when war was declared. It was lately taken over by the Government, and I suppose we all should be glad if such means of communication are available to the Government. The Government gave power to the English syndicate to construct this radio system. I understand that it has been in general use since war has been declared. It

would be interesting to the people of my county as well as the House to know to what extent it has been used and what are the circumstances that are referred to by this writer in connection with it, providing it is something that the public ought to know and it is not necessary to observe any secrecy in connection with it.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The information contained in this article, as far as I know, is quite incorrect. It is a private company, this is not one of the stations that is owned by the Government and the Government have not taken the station over. I understand that the station is not doing a commercial business yet. It connects with a station on the coast of Ireland at a place called Bally-bunnion. It is not perfect yet, but there are messages passing, and it may prove in the future of very great importance. If anything should happen to the station at Glace Bay I suppose the Militia Department thought it desirable to afford this station some protection from that standpoint, but we do not appoint the officers, and my deputy minister, who is fairly familiar with the wireless stations which the department controls at other places, says that he thinks that it is absolutely incorrect to say that any officials there are not British subjects. I am sorry I cannot give my hon. friend any more information, but it does not come within my jurisdiction.
Surely the question of flying a foreign flag in this country comes under the jurisdiction of some department of the Government?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I do not suppose for a
moment that it is true/ My attention was never called to such a thing.

I think it is a matter that
ought to be inquired into. I know that from time to time' we have seen in the newspaper press descriptions of incidents that happen in some parts of the United States when the British flag is flown on certain semi-public occasions. While I deprecate any such thing as a hostile demonstration because of the mere fact that the flag of a friendly nation is flown to the breeze, when it comes to the flying of the flag of the United States as a custom on one of our Canadian institutions in the province of New Brunswick, surely the Government ought to take some cognizance of it and inquire into the conditions under which it is permitted.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: So far as I know, there is no law in this country to prevent a citizen of Canada from flying the American flag if he chooses to do so. Perhaps we are more broad-minded in that respect than are the citizens of the United States. It is not an uncommon thing in this country in the summer season to see the American flag flying from a hotel owned by a British subject, who is thoroughly loyal to the British Crown and to Canada, out of compliment to his American guests. This is a private company.
Subsidized by the Government.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No, it has obtained nothing from our department, and it has no subsidy from the Government. This Government has not put a dollar of money into that private company, nor in any way assisted it financially. It is an English corporation; and if it chooses to % the American flag, although it may be very bad taste for that company to do so, yet there is no law in this country under which we can interfere. We live on terms of amity and good will with our friends in the United States, and I do not think we should make any complaint in regard to this matter. I do not approve of the practice of flying the American flag from hotels owned by British subjects: I would rather see our own flag flying,' that is, the British flag with the Canadian scroll upon it. I do not think, however, there is any reason for making a serious matter out of this incident. The deputy' minister informed me that all the officials were British subjects. He asks me to correct that statement. He says that one of the managers, he thinks, is an American citizen.
I do not think the illustration given by the minister is as happy as it might be. It is not a question of flying the American flag: it is a question of a doorway being draped with the American flag.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That is not so bad then.

The letter says:
So all Britishers and others entering must pass under it; also that all Canadian and British employees have been dismissed and a number of foreigners taken on instead.
The fact that the Department of Naval Service has not charge of that station i3 news to me.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Has tfhe hon. gentleman taken any steps to ascertain whether the statement in that letter is true or not ?

No. I am bringing it to the attention of the minister in order to find out whether it is true or not. The company displayed the American flag, and it is a question whether that was the proper thing to do under the present circumstances.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I do not think it is in good taste.

The minister is quite right in that. I was surprised when the minister said 'that the station was not under the control of his department. I presume, then, it is under the control of the Department of Militia and Defence ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The station belongs to a private company. The Dominion of Canada has nothing to do with its management. The Militia Department probably censors the messages it receives or sends.
.Mr. LOGGIE: I quite' appreciate the fact that it is a British company, but the minister must remember that the Government of this country gave that company its license to build a station, and in time of war it is under the control of the Government. In view of that, the Government should have seen to it that the employees were British subjects, and that the messages that go and come were censored.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: There is a censor.

Then, I suppose the
Militia Department has charge of that s'ation, and I have gone to the wrong minister for the information.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.
According to the statement of the minister, he has nothing whatever to do with the employees, and the Naval Department has not the censorship of the messages.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The censorship is in the Militia Department. I fancy my hon. friend will have to take the matter up with the Major General.
Mr. MACjjONALD:	I think my hon.
friend has come to the right quarter. It is true that the Minister of Militia has to do with the appointment of the censors; but, if I am not mistaken, the wireless telegraph people operate by virtue of licenses granted by the Department of Naval Service.
TMr. Loggie. ]
The control of those wireless offices, particularly in war-time is a matter of public interest, about which the department which grants the licenses should have something to say. I remember in the last Parliament, when hon. gentlemen opposite sat on this siae of the House, we debated for a wiiole day a resolution, which Was seriously put forward, to the effect that the use of the American flag should not be permitted at all in Canada, I would not go so far as that; but I think m a semi-Governmental institution, particularly in war-time, where for the public safety and in the interest of the nation as a whole, the control over war despatches passing through that station is vested in the Government of the day by censorship and otherwise, it is certainly bad taste to fly a foreign flag, when there are good citizens who may be sensitive about the use of such a flag. The statement is made, in this perfectly reputable paper which the minister approves, that the manager of the wireless station persisted in displaying the American flag above' his ofliee door. The writer also alleges that all Canadian and British employees have been discharged and a number of foreigners taken on instead.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
That is not so. Would
the hon. member tell me the date of the
paper?

March 24, 1915. My hon. friend probably received the paper yesterday. There is no question about one of the departments of the Government in war-time exercising some control over messages sent by any wireless station in this country. That particular institution which, to that extent at least, is under Government control, should not fly the American flag or any other flag than the British flag over its door. In the next place my hon. friend has brought forward a matter of serious complaint, that is that the control of the sending and the receiving of wireless messages by this particular station is entirely in the hands of those who are not British subjects. If it is true that those who are British subjects have been dismissed and their places filled by those who belong to a foreign country, that is a proper matter for inquiry, and the minister ought to look into it. The license being in his control, he could stop the sending of despatches at any moment. There ought to be a British flag over that station, and the people who operate there, as far as possible should be British subjects.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The operators there are all British subjects without any exception, the deputy minister informs me. At one time some Danes were employed there. They are not there now, British subjects having taken their places. That letter may or may not be true. It may be that some man has an inside room, and that he may have a British flag and an American flag in it.
The American flag is flying over the door.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
It does not appear that
the flag is flying from the building. We will, however, look into the matter.

Would the minister inform the committee in what condition the Niobe was at the outbreak of the war and what officers and crew were on her? If she was put in drydock, what repairs were necessary before she was ready to proceed to sea? And about what date was she fully equipped for sea?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The ship was in very good condition. Some of her machinery had been disconnected, and there was what you might call a nucleus crew on board. She was put in drydock, and certain work was done connecting up the machinery. She was ready for sea on the 1st of September.	*
When was her crew aboard and the vessel completely manned?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: She sailed on the 1st of September from Halifax and went to Newfoundland, and took on Newfoundland reserves of something like one hundred men who constituted part of her crew.
Does any portion of this vote go to maintain the Niobe and the Rainbow?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Not during the period of the war. I explained that before dinner.
Are these ships in commission at this time?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.
Have they fairly well performed their work since the outbreak of the war?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
So far as I know. The Niobe has been based on Halifax, and has been in and out of that port. She renders assistance, I believe, in keeping clear the trade routes. The Rainbow has been on the Pacific coast. She was fully equipped and manned at the time the war broke out. I believe she has given good satisfaction.
The Rainbow is a cruiser of 3,400 tons, and the Niobe a cruiser of 12,000 tons.
What is the speed of these ships?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: They are each about 18 knots.
The minister stated that their work was to keep clear the trade routes. I suppose that means keeping trade routes clear of the enemy's ships?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I suppose that is what the Niobe has been doing. She is based on Halifax. The Rainbow on the Pacific coast was available for any defensive operation.
The minister is confident they could give a good account of themselves should they run across a German cruiser?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That would depend on the German cruiser they ran across.
The minister is not afraid to allow these ships to get in the way of a German cruiser?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: She probably would not get in the way of any German cruiser on the Pacific, she is so much slower than they are.
All the more likely to get in the way.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: She could not overtake one, but if overtaken she could not get out of the way. She is about the same size and tonnage as the Dresden and the Leipsic, but very much slower.
The minister does not think that the men of these ships would be afraid to give battle to a German cruiser should they meet with one?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I am confident the men in the navy would not 'be afraid of anything.
They would be quite confident in engaging a German cruiser?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I could not tell what is in their mind.
They have not made complaints that the Niobe and the Rainbow were not fully equipped?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: They would not make any complaint.
The minister has no information that they are in any way afraid of the consequences in case of an engagement with the enemy?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No, I do not think a British sailor would be afraid of anything.

That is quite true. As
regards the condition of these ships and their guns and other equipment, they are all that are necessary to maintain an action against an enemy's ship?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I think that the officers and crew of the Rainbow have acted with all possible courage, and if they had got into an engagement with a German' ship they would have conducted themselves in a way to make us and the British Empire proud of them. The same is true of the officers and crew of the Rainbow, they would discharge their duties with unflinching courage. In naval warfare to-day much depends on the ship you run across. A ship of lighter armament and with smaller guns is at a disadvantage in an engagement with a ship more heavily armoured and with guns of longer range. The guns on the Niobe, while of the same calibre as the guns on the Dresden and Leipsic would not carry so far. They are guns of an older type. So, she might be hit at a range so long that she could not strike the ship engaging her.
Are these ships equipped with the same guns as before 1911?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I think so.
The minister has not taken any step to strengthen the equipment?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No. I think the Hon. gentleman does not quite understand. These ships are placed at the disposal of the Admiralty and are to-day absolutely controlled by the Admiralty; we do not interfere with the orders in any way. If the Admiralty should make a representation to us that further armament was required, I presume we should take steps at once to meet their wishes.	*
What other defences are there on the coast of British Columbia in addition to the services rendered by the Rainbow.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: There are two submarines, CC-1 andCC-2.
Owned by this Government?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes, but like the other vessels, controlled by the Admiralty.
What additional defence is there on the Atlantic coast?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I should not have said that the submarines were the only additional de-

fence on the Pacific coast. Canada owned some small boats, and these are in use. We have also had a number of British vessels on the British Columbia coast, such as the Newcastle, and two Japanese cruisers, which have been acting in concert with the naval authorities at Esquimalt. On the Atlantic coast as the hon. gentleman probably knows, a number of the vessels of the British Navy are based on Halifax and are in and out of that harbour during recent months, the Lancaster, the Essex and the Suffolk; and 1 understand that at one time the Princess Royal, one of the largest vessels of the British Navy, a vessel of the battle cruiser type, with most modern armament and capable of a speed of over thirty knots an hour, visited Halifax.
Has one of the submarines of the Canadian Government been in dry-dock?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: One had to have some repairs because on one occasion she struck the bottom. We receive daily reports as to what they are doing and they are both in the very best possible condition.
I understand that, the Niobe was repaired last summer or autumn, about the time that, the war broke out, and that she was ready for sea in September. .

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: She sailed on September 1.
How much was expended on the repairs which were made to the Niobe on that occasion?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Somewhere in the vicinity of $25,000.

What repairs were
made?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The amount which I have stated includes all repairs, dry-docking and everything else. There was nothing specially wrong with her; she was put in dry-dock chiefly as a measure of precaution, in order to see that everything was in proper shape before she sailed.
When had she been in dry-dock previously?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Not since the time she met with an accident in coming from Yarmouth. At that time extensive repairs were made; I think she had not been in dry-dock from that time until just before she sailed.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That was in the summer of 1911.

A great number of Canadian vessels are employed in the Government service in and about Halifax harbour at the present time; in fact Hah-fax has become once more a naval station, as it was in the olden 'days. In addition to the vessels of the Imperial navy, Canadian vessels, which for the time being are engaged in the naval service, are operating in that vicinity. I suggest to the minister that seafaring people of the Maritime Provinces should be encouraged to serve on these ships.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
