speechtext: The Margaret, which was a customs boat; the Canada, and the Tuna, which was presented to us by Mr. Jack Ross, are all manned by Canadians. The Canada is officered and manned by the same men as made up her crew when she was taken over and put into the naval service. The same is true of the Margaret. The Margaret was built in the Old Country for the Customs Department, and was handed over to us for naval purposes. These boats have all been of great service along the river and gulf of St. Lawrence, off Halifax, in the Atlantic and in the Bay of Fundy. The members of the crews are all Canadians.

That is true, but
what I mean is that these crews could be made the nucleus of a naval service. The men could be enlisted, as it were, into the naval service for such term of years as usually applies to such cases. I heard the minister suggest that on account of the difficulty of obtaining naval instructors, proceedings in the "way of forming a naval reserve had been somewhat retarded in the West. I am suggesting that on account of having these vessels on active but not dangerous service, an opportunity arises for taking the course to which I refer.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: When the three vessels to *which I have referred were handed over to the naval service, we could not retain the men who were on them, because the service is a voluntary service. The men nearly all volunteered, however; they have signed articles to 'Continue during the period of war if it does not last longer than three years, so that they are all enlisted as regular members of the navy at the present time.

The course I was
suggesting has been anticipated by my hon. friend, and to that extent we have in the
crews of these three vessels, seamen of the Canadian navy. I am sure that the action of Mr. Jack Ross in purchasing the steamer which he diid and in presenting it to the Canadian Government, himself volunteering for service in connection with its operations, is deserving of some remark by this committee and the House. I have no doubt that the minister will cheerfully and cordially endorse any complimentary remarks that may be made in that respect. I happen to know Mr. Ross very well, and am in a position to speak of the admirable spirit which he displayed in connection with the whole matter and the very laudable ambition which animated him and still animates him to do something, if possible, to assist Canada and the Empire upon the sea. I know that the extent to which his efforts in that direction would go is limited only by the opportunities afforded him to carry his ideas into effect. The vessel which he handed over to the Government, together with the others which are engaged in that service, are doing good work in connection with the operations in Halifax and vicinity.	"

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I fully agree with what my hon. friend has said about Mr. Eoss. This is not Mr. Ross's only patriotic act since the war broke out; no citizen-of Canada has shown a more patriotic desire to advance tlie cause of Canada and of the Empire at the present time than he has. I had intended1 making reference to this matter on Monday, when the War Bill is before the House.	,

I trust that the
minister will not feel that I anticipated in any way the formal statement which he intended to make in that regard. It might be well to note the facts in regard to the position of the Niobe of which there has been a great deal of misunderstanding. I find by the Naval Annual that the Niobe is a vessel of 11,000 tons displacement, has an armament of 16 6-inch guns, 12 12-pounders; 3 3-pounders and 2 machine guns. She is of exactly the same age, size and armament as the Ariadne, a vessel which, if I mistake not, under very gallant leadership, was especially conspicuous in the attack made on Heligoland at an earlier period of the war. She is also larger than the Berwick and the Cornwall.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The hon. member, I think, is mistaken; it was the Ar thusa.

The Ariadne was
also engaged at an earlier period of the year.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No.

The Arethusa may
have been the flagship of Admiral Beat!/, but the Ariadne was employed in attacks at the time.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I do not think so.

She was distinctly
mentioned in the press at the time. It would be wise to notice the statements contained in the Naval Annual in order to make comparisons of the size and equipment of the Niobe with many of the vessels engaged in naval warfare on the other side. I am glad to note that the minister tells us that the Niobe, when sent out to sea on December 1, was fully equipped and in a position to take her part, together with the vessels of the Imperial navy that have been on our trade routes since that time. Having been at Halifax frequently since the war began and having met naval officers who have been on British vessels that have been there, I happen to be in a position to know something of the services which have been performed but have not been published for the very reason that the operation of these vessels is not made public in the public interest. That what Canadian vessels wTe have on the Atlantic coast have been a factor, in conjunction with other vessels coming from the other side, in keeping the north Atlantic clear of German cruisers is, I am sure, a matter of gratification to every one.
Fisheries protection service-to provide for the repairs and maintenance of the fisheries protection steamers, $375,000.

I have received the following resolution passed by the municipality of the county of Richmonjl, N.S.:
Arichat, Nova Scotia,
February 27, 1915.
In the Municipal Council, Municipal County of Richmond, Jan. 16, 1915.
Resolved, that the Minister of Marine and Fisheries be memorialized by this council, to take active steps to prevent the further depredations of beam trawlers operating at night in the waters of this municipality; further
Resolved, that the minister be implored to establish a patrol to check the open violation of the federal regulations by these encroachers; and further
Resolved, that copies of this resolution be forwarded to the Hon. J. D. Hazen, Minister of Marine and Fisheries, to the federal representative, and to Messrs, J. C. Douglas and R. H. Butts.
D. H. Campbell,
Municipal Clerk.
I would ask the minister if he has received a copy of this resolution?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes, a copy of the resolution, I think, was received in the department.

This is a matter which deeply concerns the deep-fishing population in the county I represent. The subject has been discussed more or less frequently in this House and in the public press for years. We were assured by the Conservative party when in Opposition that they fully appreciated the damage which has been inflicted upon the shore fishermen in the province of Nova Scotia by these beam trawlers, and they announced by resolution at various meetings that, should their party come into power, they would take immediate steps to prohibit the use of these trawlers in the waters of the Maritime Provinces. I very much regret that their depredations are still being continued. I wish the minister would give us some assurance to-night that steps will be taken in the immediate future to prohibit the use of beam trawlers upon the coast of the Maritime Provinces.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Last year we had only two complaints in regard to trawlers having been within territorial waters. We at once carefully investigated these complaints, and the result of the investigation showed that they had not been within the three-mile limit. That, however, is not exactly what the fishermen want; they want the trawlers kept at a greater distance from the shore. If they get inside the three-mile limit it is because we do not give proper protection; but if some arrangement could be made to keep the beam trawlers a greater distance off, the fishermen believe it would be to their interest. We took this matter up with the fishery authorities of the United States and Newfoundland, and steps were taken in both countries to ascertain the effect of this beam trawling. That information has been obtained within the last two weeks. We have received a communication on ithe subject, and we believe thait within a short time it will be possible to have a conference of representatives of the United States, Newfoundland and Canada for the purpose of discussing this question and seeing what steps can be taken, by mutual arrangement., with regard to the evil complained of. That, however, leaves out of consideration the French trawler which comes across the ocean, and is absolutely within its legal right in doing so. I intended to make a statement to the House explaining the whole matter; I am having the statement prepared now, so that it may be perfectly accurate, as the matter is one

of international importance, and I shall make that statement to the House before prorogation.
1 brought the matter up tonight because, as the minister knows, we are very busy with committees, and I feared ,1 might not be present when it came before the House again.

Mr. Sinclair:
Have foreign steam trawlers been permitted to purchase coal and supplies at the Port of North Sydney, N.S., since the passing of Chapter 14 of the Acts of 1913?
Mr. J. D. Reid. Yes. The present collector at North Sydney says French steam trawlers have been permitted to purchase coal and supplies at the port of North Sydney, N.S., since he has been in office.
I got that answer on the 22nd February, this year. It contradicts the answer given by my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries a few days before, but I assume that the first answer was a blunder, because there is no doubt that French trawlers have had the free run of Canadian ports since that Act was passed. This is a great disappointment to the fishermen of the Maritime Provinces, who expected some relief from that measure, and I wish to bring the matter to the attention of the minister. I also wish to remind him of what my hon. friend from Richmond (Mr. Kyte) said, namely, that the party of hon. gentlemen opposite, in Nova Scotia at all events, took very strong ground on this question when they were out of power. They took the ground, and not only in Nova Scotia, but in the House here, that the late Government had not taken sufficient interest in the fishermen in regard to this question of steam trawling. It will be remembered that steam trawling was first commenced on the coasts of this country ifi 1908. Within two or three weeks of the arrival of the first trawlers along the coast of my own constituency, an Order in Council was passed prohibiting the operations of steam trawlers in the bays and harbours and within three miles of the coast of Canada, both east and west. That regulation has been fairly well enforced, although I understand that in certain sections it has not been absolutely enforced. The difficulty in enforcing the regulations is that these trawlers work in the night, when it is almost impossible for the cutters to watch them. But the regulation was a good one, and went a long way in the direction of assisting the fishermen. But of course it did not relate to the deep-sea fishing, which is a very important part of the industry.
At a convention of the Conservative party held at Truro in 1909, a resolution was passed to the effect that if the Conservatives came into power they would introduce measures to prevent steam trawling not only in Canadian waters, but outside of Canadian waters; and when my hon. friend introduced his Bill we thought it was in fMr. Sinclair.]
redemption of that pledge. And I must say to my hon. friend that there was a great deal of disappointment*when it was realized that the Act had been wholly inoperative during the two years after it- was passed, and that no attempt at all had been made towards putting it into force.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
When the Act was introduced I remember the speech I made and also the discussion which took place. I certainly hope we may find a way by which we can minimize the effect of the French trawlers making ports in Canada the bases for their operations, the purchase of supplies, and things of that sort. The hon. gentleman will remember that the Act referred to prevents vessels, other than those having a right by treaty, from coming into Canadian ports. When the Act was passed in 1913 representations were made by the Government of France, through their Consular Agent in Montreal, who contended that, as under the treaty with Japan the Japanese fishermen had the right to come into our ports for certain purposes, and that, as France was a favoured nation, we could not exclude French trawlers from our ports so long as the Japanese treaty was in effect. This gentleman argued that matter very strongly, and I submitted the question t-o the Minister of Justice and had several discussions with him and with the Consul of France. The result was that the Justice Department were of the opinion that, in view of the Japanese treaty, it was practically impossible for us to enforce this Act of 1913 because of the fact that France was a favoured nation and must be accorded the same rights as those which were given to Japan under the treaty to which I have referred. I think that whoever prepared the answer which my hon. friend refers to, and which was done in a hurry and without consideration, evidently had in mind that the Act had been carried out as far as it could be with regard to all Countries except those which had treaty rights. That is the difficulty that we have come up against, and it is a difficulty that it seems impossible to overcome as long as that treaty with Japan remains in existence. My hon. friend knows how in making all these treaties there is what is called a favoured nation clause under which, if any favour is given to a nation, the same advantage has to be given all other nations which have favoured nation clauses in any treaties which they may have entered into with us. That is the difficulty that confronts the

department in dealing with this question There is another way in which I am trying to deal with it and I hope it will work out in a few days. I am getting the opinion of the Department of Justice and of the Department of Customs and I trust * it will give some measure of relief.
I am afraid that if we succeeded with the United States and Newfoundland the French trawlers come in such large numbers that the effort would be useless.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The difficulty of the French trawlers could be minimized to some extent by international regulations if the different nations would enter into them. In the North sea, where they have immense numbers of trawlers, there are regulations. There is a North Sea Convention, entered into by the Governments of all the countries with the fishermen who go to the North sea, that has proved to be very efficacious there. To-day there are regulations as to the territory which shall be fished over, those regulations are laid down for the governing of everybody who fishes in the North sea, and each nation supplies a vessel for the purpose of patrolling the district and seeing that the regulations are enforced. If this could be done the difficulty which is experienced on the banks when the trawlers are fishing, and the danger under which the boat fishermen labour of having, their nets and gear destroyed by the trawlers, could be very much minimized. I think we have got to the point now where we can get a convention of that sort so far as the United States and Newfoundland are concerned. I agree with my hon. friend that there is some difficulty in regard to the French fishermen who come over every year to ply their calling on the banks of Newfoundland. If the Newfoundland Government and the United States Government enter into an agreement of this 'Sort it may be possible to bring moral pressure upon the French Government as well to agree to the pass

ing of regulations of that sort and to enter into an agreement to that effect. That is the only remedy I can see except the measure, not iso far reaching, which I hope to bring before the House. The Act of 1913 prevents any foreign fishing vessels " not permitted by treaty ot convention " from entering our ports. It is these words that have made it so difficult for us to enforce the Act as against France. At the time that I introduced the Bill I did not foresee the difficulty, and nobody in my
department foresaw it. Neither did the officials of the Justice Department. We did not have the Japanese treaty in our minds.

It would be interesting if the minister would place the opinion of the Department of Justice on the table so that we might have an opportunity of reading it, or place it on Hansard when he makes his statement.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I have no written opinion from the Department of Justice. The matter has been .discussed verbally between the Minister of Justice, the Deputy Minister of Justice, and myself, but no written opinion has been given to us. Perhaps I should not say that an absolute opinion has been come to, but the opinion they had upon it was that it would not be desirable for us to proceed to enforce the law in view of the Japanese treaty. It is desirable to have the opinion, but perhaps it is not well to press an opinion of that sort too strongly at the present time.

If we have any legal rights it is well that we should know it. In dealing with this question I think the proper course would be to reserve certain territory at sea in which steam trawling would be absolutely prohibited. We cannot expect to get the French nation, or any ioreign nation, to agree that the whole Atlantic ocean shall be withdrawn from the operation of fishing vessels.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: But we might get them to agree to regulations.

The gulf of St. Lawrence, which is the great breeding ground of the fish, might be reserved. I think that would be a reasonable request. The gulf of St. Lawrence is surrounded by British territory, and it is really an inland sea belonging to Canada. It was a great misfortune, -when these bays were defined in the convention at the1 Hague, that the gulf of St. Lawrence was not included among Canadian waters. If the gulf of St. Lawrence could be withdrawn from the use of steam trawlers that would be a great step in advance. But the place where they are operating most is at the Banks. Would it not be a fair proposal to ask that the Banks should be withdrawn from the operation of trawlers? There are certain areas along the coast of Nova Scotia that I think might be regarded as the breeding grounds of cod and haddock, and we might fairly ask that these be withdrawn from the operation of trawlers in the

same way that the sealing question has been dealt with on the Pacific coast. It -has been agreed by Japan, the United States and Great Britain that -seals shall not be killed in certain waters. Fish are just as important. If my hon. friend, in dealing with this question, can -succeed in withdrawing these waters from the use of steam trawlers and allow the trawlers to operate in the rest of the Atlantic ocean, he will have taken a gre-at -step forward even if he cannot go any further. If there are	any documents to	show whatthe legal position of this question is	I would like	to	see	them.
If there are any reports or communications from the United States which my hon. friend can place on the table at the time he addresses the House on the question, they will also be very acceptable.

The minister stated that his department had received only two complaints last year in regard to a violation of the regulations prohibiting the operation of steam trawlers within the three-mile limit. When he makes his statement to the House, has he a statement to make with respect to that question also, and does he desire that I do not discuss it now? *

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I am quite willing that my hon. friend discuss it now.
I am not particularly anxious to do so, but I do not know whether or not the minister wants us to discuss it at this stage.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I do not want to shut off discussion at any stage.
Shall I have an opportunity when the minister makes his statement?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Yes.
Fisheries protection service-to provide for new vessels, $30,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: This vote is for the fisheries protection service on lake Erie. Tne-department, in order to carry out efficiently the fisheries protection work on lake 'Erie, considers that a vessel is required to work in conjunction with the Vigilant, now employed on that service. Inquiries have been made into the matter, and it has been decided to obtain a small vessel which will be more suitable for work around the islands at the end of the lake. It is also proposed to build such a vessel, and designs and specifications have been prepared by the naval architect.
Is she to be built in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes. The policy of this Government is to build all our vessels in Canada.
Under contract?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
When I say "under contract," there are some vessels that we build at the shipyards -at Sorel. We have a great many men employed there doing repair work, and I think the work is being very well done.
Hydrographic surveys, including the survey of Hudson bay, $390,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The details of this expenditure are: James bay, $30,000; lake Ontario, $30,000; lake Superior, $30,000; the lower St. Lawrence river, $50,000; the Pacific coast, $100,000; the Atlantic coast, $70,000; harbour surveys, $20,000; automatic gauges, $25,000; general amount, $35,000.

How much for Hudson
bay?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We have done a considerable amount of work in Hudson bay. We have port Nelson charted and the waters outside port Nelson. We have also charted part of the lower portion of James bay, and the work there has been proceeded with. There is more work, of course, that will have to be done in the future, but very good progress has been made. There is great necessity for work on the lower St. Lawrence and also for work on the Atlantic coast at the present time.
What is the depth of water at port Nelson?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I cannot tell my hon. friend, because I have not the chart here.
What size of ship can come into port Nelson without dredging further? -

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: At high water vessels can come in that draw from 20 to 25 feet. There is one point where at low water there is only 20 feet of water. A vessel of greater draught than that would have to wait until high tide before coming in.
What tide is there?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Seventeen feet.

Is the survey at port Nelson merely with a view to acquire a knowledge of the conditions as they are, or is it being made with a view of -the improvement

of those countries in the way of creating a harbour?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The hydrographic survey
is for the purpose of obtaining accurate knowledge of conditions as they are. It has nothing to do with the work of building or enlarging or dredging harbours; but it affords information that is available to every shipmaster visiting the port, and also information of which the department, which has to do with the management and building and creation of harbours, can avail itself, in order to know what should be done to render the port safe for navigation. The information we have is available to the Department of Railways and to the Department of Public Works. The Department of Railways is carrying on the terminal works at Port Nelson in connection with the Hudson Bay railway. The object of the hydrographic survey is to have accurate charts so as to show the mariners just what the conditions of the waters are along the coast and in the harbour.
Is the minister able to say in short terms to the committee what is the condition of access to Port Nelson at the present time?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I cannot do so with any
degree of accuracy without having the chart here. I shall be very happy to send copies of the chart to my hon. friend.

I should be very glad to '
have them, and I would appreciate the courtesy of the minister in sending them. That, however, is hardly the point to be arrived at. I am quite aware that the minister will say, as he has already said, that if we want information in regard to the projects of the Government regarding Port Nelson, we must apply to the Railway Department; but from the fact that the Naval Department has information as to conditions as they are, it must be possible to draw from a knowledge of those conditions what improvements will be necessary in order to establish Port Nelson as a suitable ocean port. It is not a matter of idle curiosity; it is a matter of very far-reaching importance to the people of the prairie West, particularly in view of the criticisms that are being made from time to time with regard to the project of the Hudson Bay railway.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service

speechtext: Has the report been sent out?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes. Every member has it.

Did you find any depth
of water suitable for a harbour at the lower end of James bay.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: There is plenty of depth of water in the lower end of the bay. If my hon. friend would like to see the charts, we will send them to him.
Which is the lower end of the bay, the southern?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I should say the southern end. The James bay survey was in charge of Mr. Jobin, who left Ottawa on the 18th of April and went down the Moose river from Cochrane, Ont. His instructions were to survey the mouth of the Moose river and a portion of the East coast of the bay to ascertain if a harbour could be found at Snake point. He was successful in finding what might be made a very fair harbour. Moose river empties into the bay at the lower end.
Has anything been done about the navigation of the straits?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes, we had a party there last year. That comes under the marine vote. My recollection is that we have had twelve beacons placed in the straits and a wireless telegraph station established at Port Nelson and one at Le Pas, and provision made for a wireless telegraph station on the straits to communicate with Port Nelson and Le Pas.
Has the minister any plans to increase the number of wireless stations on the coast of the Maritime Provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I would be glad to tell my hon. friend privately. Certain work has gone on there in connection with the war which it is not desirable to make public.
What is the experience of the navigation of Hudson straits; how long is the navigation season?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I do not profess to give exact information. Last year was an unusually bad season in the straits; navigation conditions differ there from year to year. I find it stated here:
The serious ice condition found at the west entrance to Hudson strait, north of Mansel island, during- October, is most exceptional and hard to account for. There is little or no tide and current at this point, and a mass of ice once caught would be very likely to remain. As a rule the Fox channel ice never remains long during the season, but passes out of the strait.
That is, the ice from the north.
During the summer of 1912, little or no ice came down, being a fine calm season, and even on the 2nd November the Minto found no ice in this passage. On the contrary, during the past season, extremely and exceptionally heavy northerly winds prevailed, which would have a tendency to carry a great quantity of ice down. An ordinary freight vessel could not for a moment have attempted a passage when the Acadia passed out.
There is no information on hand concerning the passage south and east of Mansel island, and it may possibly have been clear of ice. When the Acadia arrived off the north end it was rather late in the season, and too expensive on coal to risk a trip around to explore. If the navigation into Hudson bay and and straits warrants the-expense, by operating a powerful tug equipped with wireless in connection with a wireless station on the north end of Mansel island, masters of ships could be kept informed regarding the ice conditions, and conduct themselves accordingly.
Would the navigation season last, for three months?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I do not like to speak definitely, but I do not think it would be three months on the average.
Would the season be in June, July and August?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No, later than that. Sometimes navigation may commence in July, but it is usually August, and may continue during September and October.
What is the nature of the ice encountered-icebergs?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Sometimes the place is filled with ice, so that a vessel would have to cut its way through. I have a picture on my desk of the Acadia taken in August last in the straits, and there is ice all around it. Conditions last year were worse than usual.
How long was Captain Anderson up there last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: He appears to have reached Port Nelson on August 19. He left Port Nelson October 19 for Halifax and the remark is entered in the report that Port Nelson harbour was full of ice. I find that the Bellaventure arrived there August 10 and departed August 22, for Halifax. The Sinbad arrived September 4 with coal and left October 1 for Sydney, but returned again on October 8, as the passage was blocked by ice. The Alette arrived on September 13 with scow and lumber. She departed from Port Nelson October 7, but returned again October 14 in a sinking condition, having been 'damaged by ice off Mansel island. The ship was beached and the crew returned in the Government steamer Acadia.
Was there much field ice there in August?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: In the season of 1913.
They appear to have encountered ice every month.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Yes.
Mr. -SINCLAIR: What happened to the dredge that was wrecked in Hudson bay, about which we heard something at the last session of the House?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I always understood that it was not wrecked. The Minister of Railways can give you more accurate information than I can.
I suppose very little business is done at Port Nelson at present?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Fur trading may be carried on to some extent but, I should think, nothing else.

I must say that I am very much disappointed at the report which the minister has just read. I have taken a very great interest in the Hudson bay route; I have read almost everything in connection with it that I could get my hands on; but this is certainly the most discouraging report that I have seen or heard. I have talked with men who have been there; I have read reports made by men who have been in that country for twenty-fiye or thirty years, a great many
of whom assert that Hudson bay and the Hudson strait are open to navigation for eight to ten months in each year. I believe that their reports are absolutely correct. Captain Anderson has not given us a fair deal in the report which he has made in regard to the Hudson bay route.

So far as the navigation of Hudson strait is concerned, that is a matter that wo have to leave to Providence; we cannot change it, and the best we can do is to take it as it is and make the best we can of it. As to whether navigation is open for one month, two months, three months or six months, that is not the point. The point is that the trade of a vast country has been carried through those straits for a period of 200 years and can be carried through them for 200 years longer, if facilities corresponding to the requirements of advanced civilization are provided. What can be controlled are the facilities for reaching the bay and the harbour facilities at the bay, and it is in regard to that matter that we ask the minister for information. How far from the shore line does the general depth of the water become sufficient for floating large vessels?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I think the deep water is some distance out; I do not know how many miles.
My information is that it is a very considerable distance out.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It is all on the chart.

I am quite aware of that, but the point I want to make is this. The information on which I have based my opinion is that the difficulties in the way of making a harbour at Port Nelson are very great, while there is at Fort Churchill a natural harbour, requiring practically no expenditure in order to give facilities for loading and unloading vessels of the greatest draught. I have not in any way found fault with the Government for making the choice of Port Nelson as against Fort Churchill, but I want to get plainly before the committee and the country the fact that in doing so they gratuitously laid upon the enterprise of the Hudson Bay railway a vast and unnecessary burden. Having done this, I think it is their business to take such measures and to make such expenditures as will make Port Nelson a suitable port for carrying on the traffic of Hudson bay. I have been anxious to know what the plans of the Government are in regard to that

port; how long it will take to complete these plans and what the expenditure upon them will be. I am quite aware that these questions are not to be addressed to my hon. friend, but as he has already said that the information acquired by his department is the information upon which the Public Works Department and the Department of Railways must base their plans, I would, have thought that it would be within his knowledge as to whether the Government of which he is a member have made such plans, and, if they are adequate, how long they will take to complete and what their cost will be; or if the fact is that we are committed to the establishment and creation of a port at Port Nelson without any such plans having been formulated or without any such estimate of expenditure having been made, or any period of time having been decided upon for the completion of this work. I am as strongly in favour of the Hudson bay road as the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. W. H. Sharpe) or anybody else. I believe that the welfare of the West is intimately dependent upon the successful completion of the railway and port and the successful operation of the road. My fear is that unless this question of the port is taken hold of and handled energetically and the work completed adequately and in good time, the whole project will be unduly discredited, not because of the natural features but because of lack of due consideration in dealing with this port question, a question which need not have arisen if the railway had been carried to Fort Churchill. Now that it has been decided to carry the railroad to Port Nelson the responsibility is on the Government, and I am desirous of impressing strongly on them the measure of that responsibility, because upon what they do at Port Nelson, the time in which they do it, and the cost of doing it, depends in large measure the success or failure of the Hudson Bay Railway project.
How far from the mouth of the Nelson river is it necessary to go out in the bay in order to get say 30 feet of water.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I could not say without having the chart here. Right in the harbour of Port Nelson I believe there is 30 feet of water.

The reports from men
who have been there are that you have to go a considerable distance,

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Ships of considerable size go in now.
The Minto could not do that.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The Minto did so.
Is that really on record?

I remember talking
about the matter with the late Minister of Railways who sent Mr. Armstrong, an engineer, to go over the country very carefully to examine the harbours in connection with the railway, and I understood that he had reported that there was an outlet to Port Nelson, although it was a somewhat tortuous channel. It is one not ordinarily known to navigators of ships who prefer to lie outside and send the small boats ashore.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service

speechtext:
No doubt there is a
report in the Department from Mr. Armstrong giving full information on the subject.
Radiotelegraph service-to provide for the building and maintenance of wireless stations, $350,000.
Mr. OLiVER: I have heard the minister say he proposed to establish a wireless station on Hudson bay. Owing to the fact that the flow of ice varies from year to year and from time to time within the one season, I would think there should be more than one station. [DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I agree that there should
be more than one and v/e have a scheme worked out in the department which provides ultimately for three. We hope to work up to that and within the next three years to establish three stations there.
Tidal stations and surveying steamers, $35,000.
Are those new stations?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
These are small observation stations. They are changed about from year to year. This year many of them will be in British Columbia. This service includes the preparation of tide-tables, etc.
Patrol of the northern waters of Canada, $50,000.
What is the latest information the Government has in regard to the Stefansson expedition and what are their intentions in regard to it?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The Karluk sank on
January 11. Those who were on board of her before she sank were Mr. Stefansson, Mr. Jenness, anthropologist, Mr. McConnell, meteorologist, Mr. Wilkins, photographer, and some of the crew. The scientific party and crew then camped on the ice.
Crushed in by the ice?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Yes. On January 21, 1914, an advance party composed of Alex. Anderson, Charles Barker, John Brady and A. King started from the camp to effect a landing on Herald island. Nothing has since been heard from this party. On February 5, 1914, a .second party composed of Messrs. McKay, Murray, Beauchet and Morris left camp. Nothing has since been heard of them. A third party left on March 12, 1914, and landed on Wrangel island. The third party, which reached Wrangel island on the 12th March, was composed of O. Malloch, geologist; S. Mamen, assistant geologist; W. McKinley, magneticdan; R. U. Bartlett, captain; John Munro, first engineer; Robert Williamson, second engineer; F. M. Mauxier, fireman; L. W. Breddy, fireman; H. Williams, A.B.; R. Templeman, steward; E. F. Chafe, cabin hoy; and John Hadley, utility man. This party was under the command of Captain Bartlett, who is well known as a very skilful and experienced navigator in northern regions. All these men, with the exception of Messrs. Mamen and Malloch, who died from nephritis, and Breddy, who was accidentally -shot, were rescued by the King and Wing on September 7, 1914, and by the cordial assistance of the United States Government were landed safely at Victoria by the United States revenue cutter Bear. These men left Wrangel island and got over to the coast of Alaska. Captain Bartlett made his way down the coast and got word to us. We immediately got into communication with the United States Government, with the result that the revenue cutter Bear was sent out to bring the men down to Victoria.
Special attention is called by the officer of the department to the heroic behaviour of Captain Bartlett, not only for the manner in which he disciplined those under his command under most trying circumstances, *but also for his bravery in journeying over 160 miles of Arctic ice to rescue those who were stranded on "Wrangel island. Mr. Stefansson joined the southern party at Collinson point on March 8, as after leaving the Karluk he first made a trip to Herschel island to dispatch mail, and thence to the Mackenzie Delta
and Fort MacPherson for the purpose of scientific exploration. The scientific investigations of the southern party carried on during the winter of 1913-14 were most successful. Many new specimens have been obtained and forwarded to Ottawa for further investigation. I may say that since that time nothing has been heard of Stefansson. On March 22, 1914, accompanied by Messrs. Johnston, marine biologist; Mr. McConnell, secretary; Wilkins, official photographer; Bernard, Castleton, Crawford, Starkerson and Anderson, Stefansson started on a trip across the ice for the purpose of taking scientific observations, and of attempting to discover a new land or polar continental shelf. Of these men, Messrs. Wilkins, Bernard and Castleton, returned to camp. Later on Messrs. Johnston, McConnell and Crawford returned and reported that on March 23 the ice broke off and drifted eastward eighty miles in one night. They left Starkerson and Anderson with Mr. Stefansson. That was the last heard of Stefansson. There is a possibility that Stefansson may have got across to Siberia and may be heard from some day. The different parties out there, in fact, everybody going to the north, are keeping their eyes open and doing everything they can to find him. I had a long talk with Captain Bartlett, who came to Ottawa some months ago. He is a most experienced navigator in northern waters, and belongs to a family of experienced navigators. They are Newfoundland people. I think he was with Peary at the time he discovered the Pole. Bartlett thinks there is a possibility of Stefansson being found, if he has not already perished. He says Stefansson was a most experienced and resourceful man who would get along if anybody could. There is a possibility, but I am afraid it is only a possibility and not a probability, that Stefansson may be found.
Is the distance to Siberia very great?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It is about 1,100 miles from the point where Stefansson was last seen.
The minister has mentioned several interesting specimens. What do they consist off?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: They have been sent here, but I understand have not been classified by the officers of the Geological Department. When they have been classified they will be put in the museum.
What part did this Government take in securing the rescue of the party which reached Wrangel island, and were afterwards rescued by the King & Wing ?	*

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We knew nothing about it until we heard from Captain Bartlett. As soon as he sent word to us we got into touch with all the vessels that we learned were up in the North and with the United States Government and the Russian Government, which have vessels up in that neighbourhood. They at once went to their relief. The department has paid some bills that were incurred by one of these ships in bringing the party across to the mainland. We took immediate and prompt action as soon as we heard from Captain Bartlett and, as I said, communicated with the Russian and United States Governments. The United States Government rendered us very valuable aid with their revenue cutter Bear, which was up there.

Was the United States
Government paid for their services?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: They would not accept anything.
Was the Norwegian boat paid that actually made the rescue?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes, they were paid. That was the King & Wing.
Were they paid in a manner creditable to the Government?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It was certainly satisfactory to them, and I think it was a proper sum that we paid.

Has the Government in
mind any active steps to be taken in regard to Stefansson and the men who are with him ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
We have three ships up
there now searching for them: the North Star, the Alaska, and the Mary Sachs. We are doing everything that we think can be done, but as the hon. gentleman knows it is not an easy situation. These three ships have instructions to search and do all they can to find them.
These three ships are still up there?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.

The reason I press this
point is that I have seen an article in Harper's magazine, which I can only construe

as reflecting seriously upon this Government, for not taking more active measures looking to the relief of Stefansson and of those parties who have not been heard from since they left the Karluk.
I do not wish to unduly criticise, hut I must say that, taking the facts that have been presented to us from time to time by the minister, reading the accounts I have seen in the newspapers and reading this article by a friend of Stefansson-

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Is that McConnell?

I think so-I am bound to say that the facts do not reflect any credit upon Canada or upon the Government. This expedition was sent out on the responsibility of the Government of Canada, and it is presumed that, it was intended to serve a useful purpose. The leader of the expedition has some reputation in that line. It has been usual under such circumstances by the Governments of other countries to take more notice of the misfortunes that have happened to their explorers than has been taken in this case. It may be that the Government is misjudged. I am not concerned so much about that, but the reflections that have appeared are reflections upon Canada as a whole. If the minister has any information that he can give to this House as to greater activity, on the part of the Government in seeking to relieve the situation of these explorers, he would certainly be very well advised to place it before khe House. Not to speak too strongly, it seems to me that there has been a very cold-blooded view taken of the case, and I think it would be entirely creditable to the country, as well as to the Government, if some more active measures than have been taken in the past were taken on the direct responsibility of the Government looking to the relief of these people.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
This matter has been very carefully considered, and everything has been done up to the present time that can be done. It was considered by officials of the department and by many scientific men, knowing to a considerable extent the conditions that prevail there, and they think that everything has been done that can be dpne. I know there was something in an American paper, and I know a gentleman came here who wanted us to undertake an expedition by means of aeroplanes that would have cost hundreds of thousands of dollars. The proposition was carefully considered by the department, and the department believed there was nothing practical

about it, and that no good could result from it, and they declined it. It was after this that we saw these criticisms to which the hon. gentleman has referred. The officials thought that an expedition to go out with aeroplanes to search in the Arctic for Stefansson was absolutely impracticable, and was not one that would give any good results. That is the only proposition that has been made. We considered everything we could do. We are just as anxious as my hon. friend or anybody else to do everything we can for these unfortunate men. Even if Stefansson is lost, which I am afraid is the case, we would like to make a search to definitely ascertain that fact. We have three vessels up there, there are other vessels which know everything about it and I am satisfied that everything is being done that could be done in connection with the matter. It was considered with the greatest possible care, and the seriousness of the situation appeared to everybody. It was considered not only by the deputy minister but by other officials in connection with the department, and the conclusion they came to was that everything that possibly could be done of a practical character has been done in connection with the matter.
Rewards for saving- life, including lifesaving stations, $125,400.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: This is a transfer. The lifesaving stations have been placed under the control of the Naval Service Department. This vote used to appear in the Marine Estimates. It is really no addition to the Estimates.
The amount is the same?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Exactly the same.
Is there any increase in the number of stations?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Under this vote $17,200 is spent in British Columbia and $25,500 in Ontario, $10,000 in New Brunswick, $26,600 in Nova Scotia, $2,600 in Prince Edward Island, and, on general account, $6,500. That is for maintenance. A new building is being erected at Point Pelee, Ontario, costing $10,500. There is a general vote for new -boats, and repairs to buildings of $30,000, making the total $125,400. The stations in Nova Scotia are Bakers Cove, Blanche, Clark Harbour, Canso, Devil Island, Port Mouton, Scattari, Seal Island, St. Paul Island, Whitehead, Sable Island, Cheticamp, and Bay View. Some are permanent and some volunteer stations. The 103
stations, in New Brunswick are at Little Wood Island, Richibucto, Port Escuminac and Cape Tormentine.
What is the difference between a volunteer and a permanent station ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: A permanent station i3 where the men are there permanently, ready at a moment's notice to go out to sea.
They are paid every day in the year?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Paid for the season during which they are there. A volunteer station is a station where men living in the neighbourhood pursue their ordinary avocations and when a wreck occurs they go and man the lifeboats. They are not paid so much a day, but for the number of drills they do during the season.
Have any new buildings been erected at Cheticamp during the last season?	"

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: There is one being built now.
Was it put up to tender?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I understand it is a very small building, costing with the land $425.
Who built it?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: William AuCoin.
Is the hon. gentleman sure of that?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It is an AuCoin anyway.

I suppose there are five hundred of them down there. I may tell the hon. gentleman it was Alexander AuCoin. What system did the minister follow in giving an expenditure of $450 to one individual without tender and con-contract.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
It was an arrangement that was made, I understand, by Admiral Kingsmill, who Went down there >and decided upon the ground. That probably was the cheapest way of doing it. The land was secured from the man who put up the building. As I understand it, he gave the land and put up the building for $425. I think Admiral Kingsmill came to the conclusion that that was the cheapest way out of the matter, because if he had not given the man the job of putting up the building, the land would have cost a great deal more. Putting the two together, Ad-



miral Kingsmill thought he was making a good bargain. The matter never came to my attention before to-night. I have just picked up the information about it here.
What is the size of the building P

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It is a double-boarded house with a stone foundation, and is large enough to serve as a living place for a crew of eight or ten men. I cannot tell the size.
Was any protest made against giving this work to Mr. AuCoin ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I certainly never had it called to my attention, and my officials here say that they never heard of it.

I have taken particular interest in this station. In fact, I give myself credit for having initiated the idea of having it put there. The late Government made provision for the erection of a istation. I recognized that there was a great necessity for a life-saving station in that particular part of the county, inasmuch as the people are exclusively fishermen, ana rne coast is very rough. At the time the engineer went down there first to select a site for the station, I recommended to him a man by the name of Mr. Doucett for coxswain, or captain of the boat, as they name it 'down there. The change of Government came afterwards, and the friends of my hon. friend the minister made the .recommendation that this man be dismissed and another man be appointed in his stead, a gentleman by the name of Mr. Maillet. Mr. Maillet, I must say, was a very suitable man.
Was he a Tory ?

Yes. I have nothing at all to say against him. Shortly afterwards trouble arose between Mr. Maillet and one of the crew, Mr. Cormier. Mr. Cormier was dismissed by one of the officers of the department, I think Commander Thompson. An investigation was asked for, and Mr. Nickerson, who is also an officer of the department, was sent down to investigate thi matter. He made certain recommendations. At the investigation, however, counter charges were made hy Cormier against Maillet, who was captain. Mr. Nickerson investigated the charges and the counter charges. His report I find in t1 return I have here. He exonerates both parties from any very serious guilt. He says:

In my opinion, the complaint against Cormier as contained in the coxswain's letter to you is by no means sustained in all its gravity, while the counter charge is a trifling matter indeed, a sort of trumpery accusation quite easily accounted for.
That is the opinion of Mr. Nickerson with regard to Mr. Maillet. I moved for this return 'some time ago, and looking over it from cover to cover, I find that there is nothing against Mr. Maillet. I propose, however, following the various pages here. The next thing I^find is that Mr. Cormier was reinstated, and that my opponent, Mr. Gallant a thorough gentleman, I must say, but of course a very strong Tory, recommended the dismissal of Mr. Maillet forthwith. The minister in reply to him stated that, in his judgment, the was no justification for the dismissal of Mr. Mail-let. The hon. minister said what was Tight, that one of his officers, who went down there and investigated the case, stated that there was nothing to justify his dismissal such a short time after his appointment. In that the minister was thoroughly correct. He had the interest of the station at' heart then; and had he continued to occupy that position with respect to this case, it would have been better for the station and for all concerned. Another officer, however, was sent down, namely, Admiral Kingsmill. He also made a report. I am going to put his report upon Hansard. He addressed the report to the department:
With reference to your memorandum of 31st August, I beg to report that I visited this station on the 15th of October and found that Mr. Gallant, who makes the charges against the coxswain was not there, but I interviewed several people and found that there is a feeling that the coxswain is not loyal to the Government who gave him his appointment.
I would hardly think that a man in the position that Admiral Kingsmill occupies would be sent down there to determine the politics of this man. He would be' sent down for technical purposes, to find out whether the station was satisfactory, and so forth. The report continues:
I would submit that there is no reason for retaining him in the appointment; he is not able to manage his boat's crew, and the station is most untidy and ill-kept. When the station is closed down at the close of navigation, I would suggest that some one be nominated to take charge, make an inventory and lock the boathouse up until the re-opening of navigation, when the new coxswain and crew should be appointed. None of the crew made any complaint to me against the coxswain, and he himself spoke such indifferent English that I could

not gather from him any reason for the trouble which had taken place.
Mr. Maillet is a Frenchman and speaks French very well. I do not know whether Admiral Kingsmill .speaks French or not.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: What is the hon. gentleman reading from?

From sessional papers, No. 159, page 41. I want to point out particularly with respect to Admiral Kingsmill's report that, in my judgment, he would have done much better had he got some further information than he seems to have secured down there. He says he met several of the people there; but what strikes me very forcibly is that, notwithstanding the fact that there is previous to this report a statement by the crew of the life-saving station setting forth the charges against this man Maillet, at the time when one of the officers of the department went down to investigate the case, those men had no complaint to make. I would think that if they had made a complaint-and I doubt it very much- against Mr. Maillet, when the officers of the department went down there, they should have been able to substantiate the charges. I find from the report of Admiral Kingsmill that they made no charges at all in his presence.
I find a report here from the Deputy Minister of Naval Affairs covering a communication which is addressed to Mr. Gallant. It points out again that the officers of the life-saving station, when called upon to give evidence, had no evidence to give.
I infer from the correspondence that the dismissal is the result of nothing more or less than a desire on the part of Mr. Gallant to dismiss the man whom he himself had appointed only a few months before. As to the politics of Mr. Maillet I know nothing. I had assumed that he was a strong Conservative and a supporter of Mr. Gallant. Evidently Mr. Gallant had suspicions, and the investigation of Admiral Kingsmill was to determine what the politics of this man were and not what his efficiency was.
I find a report by Admiral Kingsmill in which he says that he interviewed a certain gentleman down there, who, he says is the leading man in the community, and this gentleman told him that so far as he knew Mr. Maillet was as good a man as they were likely to get, but the opinion in this ease was that he was not loyal to the Government from whom he received his appointment. Here is another reference to this
man's politics. My only reason for bringing this before the committee is that I fear the virus of politics has been injected into this institution. I fear that there is very little prospect that this life-saving station can give the service which I hoped it would give. It is true, there was a little disturbance between these two men. But I can assure the minister that if he were down in Cheticamp, he would find an equally great disturbance between two other men; and I suppose the next thing will be the dismissal of more men because of this little difference that could have been settled simply by not listening to either party but insisting that each should do his duty in his position. I hope the minister will not give heed too readily to these representations made by men who are actuated, in my judgment, by no other desire than to give way to their political feelings. This is evident from the first page of the report to the last. I have taken up the time of the committee believing that the service may be benefited by the minister being placed in possession of the facts.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I do not wish to take up time unnecessarily; but my hon friend from Inverness (Mr. A. W. Chisholm) seems to think that this man was dismissed because of his politics. That question did not enter into it at all. This man was recommended for this position by Mr. Gallant, who was the Conservative candidate for Inverness in 1911, and appointed to the position largely on his recommendation. So far as I know the man was a Conservative, and there was no charge against him that he had interfered in politics. There was trouble at the station; discipline did not seem to be enforced by Mr. Maillet; and he made a charge against Mr. Cormier, one of his crew, and Mr. Cormier retaliated by making charges against him. Mr. Nickerson, an official of the Fisheries Department in Nova Scotia, was asked to make a report. He visited the place, and reported that in his opinion the complaint against Mr. Cormier contained in the coxswain's letter to Commander Thompson was by no means sustained in all its gravity, while the counter-charge was " a trifling matter indeed-a sort of trumpery accusation quite easily accounted for"-meaning, I suppose, that the coxswain had made a charge that was not sustained against this man, and the man retaliated by making charges against the coxswain. Mr. Nickerson proceeds to praise both men:
16J6

Maillet is no doubt a capable boatman. Cormier, I believe, is a trustworthy watchman. A slight personal pique was the beginning of the trouble which has been wretchedly augmented by outside interference into which it was not judicious for me to inquire, but which
was obvious enough______Much has been doneto place this Cheticamp station on a high plane of usefulness. The location is correct, the outposts are properly chosen, the equipment is good and the men well qualified. Order and discipline can be introduced and maintained here if the crew are more fully instructed as to the nature of their duties in every part ot the service. They are as yet new to the work.
Still, discipline did not prevail at this station; the coxswain did not enforce the authority he had, and constant bickering and trouble existed between himself and the crew. Representations were made about the matter, and I instructed Admiral Kingsmill, whose duty it is, to look into the matter and report what should be done. Admiral Kingsmill, I am sure, did not have any thought of politics. Being a civil servant, I suppose he has no politics, but if he had any, I presume they would lead him to sympathize with hon. gentlemen opposite. He went to this station and investigated, and he reports:
With reference to your memo, of 31st of August; I beg to report that I visited this station on the 15th October and found that Mr. Gallant, who makes the charges against the coxswain, was not there, but I interviewed several people and found that there is a feeling that the coxswain is not loyal to the Government who gave him his appointment.
I take that to mean, not that he was not loyal to the Administration, but that he was not loyal to the Government of the country, and was not doing his duty in his position. Admiral Kingsmill had no instructions to inquire into the man s politics; there is no charge of political interference connected with the matter. He says:
1 would submit that there is no reason for retaining him in the appointment; he is not able to manage his boat's crew and the station is most untidy and ill-kept.
That is the report which induced me to take the action I did. That the coxswain was not able to manage his boat's crew is clear from the trouble that arose, each making charges against the other. Admiral Kingsmill further says:
When the station is closed down at the close of navigation, I would suggest some one be appointed to take charge of it, make an inventory and lock the boathouse up till the reopening of navigation, when the new coxswain and crew should be appointed. None of the crew made any complaint to me against the coxswain, and he himself spoke such indifferent

English that I could not gather from him any reason for the trouble which had taken place.
Perhaps that was one trouble, that he could not make his views and wishes well known to his crew. Or were they all people who understood French?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
That is the report on which this man was relieved of his position. There was no politics in it so far as the department was concerned, and no charge made of political interference. This man was appointed largely on the recommendation of the man who was the Conservative candidate for Inverness.
Admiral Kingsmill is presumed to know his business; he is a trained and experienced officer. Doss my hon. friend think that it would be good business to keep in office as coxswain a man who cannot, enforce discipline with his crew and who allows his station to be ill-kept and dirty, as reported by Admiral Kingsmill? So far as I was concerned the question of the man's politics never entered into the matter.

The moment Mr. Maillet tried to enforce the regulations sent to him by my hon. friend's department, he incurred the enmity of the crew. The charges that were being made by the crew of the station were not laid before Admiral Kingsmill when he went down there, because the Admiral says that the crew had no charges to make. The same may be said in respect of Mr. Nicholson's visit. The crew of the station did not make their charges against the captain while the officers were there, showing conclusively that the whole thing was manufactured by politicians. My hon. friend's interpretation of Admiral Kingsmill's reference to politics does not correspond with mine. So long as the department refuses to help the captain of the life-saving station to carry out the regulations, so long will the station fail to produce	the results I had
hoped that it would produce. This man Maillet made an honest effort to carry out the instructions sent to him by the department, and thereby made himself un popular with the crew. The crew and their friends sent representations here which were false, and which they dared , not make when my hon, friend's representatives were down there. The matter is in the minister's hands.

Mr. A. A. McLEAN; I shoulcl like to bring to the attention of the minister a report which was current in the Maritime Provinces last year. A very severe storm occurred in Northumberland strait, and the report reached Charlottetown that a vessel was in distress between cape Tormentine and cape Traverse. The marine agent at Charlottetown sent the lifeboat to relieve the distressed vessel. The lifeboat could not get there unaided, and was towed by a tug. On the way out in the height of the storm, the crew went on board the tug, and shortly afterwards the lifeboat upset. If the crew had been on board the lifeboat, they would have been drowned. What I want to bring to the attention of the minister is the fact that it is currently stated that the boats which are supplied are not suitable for the purposes of life-saving stations. There is no use in maintaining life-saving stations at great expense if the boats supplied are not of the proper type.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The boat belonged to what live-saving station?

Charlottetown. I took
occasion to ask some of the men who were on board the boat about this matter, and they told me-they are men who have been at sea for many years, and know something about these things-that in their opinion the boat was not of the proper type. I think that the department should take this matter up, because the material supplied to men who are engaged in saving life should be of the very highest quality in order that they may be able to render all possible assistance to vessels which may be in distress, without at the same time endangering their own lives. This is, perhaps, more important than any of the other matters that have been brought to the attention of the committee. I am not myself expressing any opinion as to the facts, because I am not' posted on the subject, but it is currently reported that the boats are not of the proper type and are not as good as those used in England or on the continent of Europe. If that is the case, I think the Government ought to take the matter up and see that it is adjusted.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I entirely agree with my hon. friend that if you are going to have lifeboats you want to have boats that will do the work which they are intended to do. I will certainly make inquiry into the case of the lifeboat of the Charlottetown station, and if it is not suitable for the purposes for
which it is intended, I will take steps to have it replaced by a suitable boat.
The complaint is made in this report that the lifeboat is not adequate enough; I call the minister's attention to that fact.
A lifeboat should be self-baling and self-righting.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It ought to be self-righting. Is this boat an old boat?
It is an old boat. I understand that the boat at Cape Tormentine is of the same type, and is of very little use.
I have some complaint to make about the boat at the Souris station.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Is that an old boat?

It has been in use seven or eight years, I think. It is said that this boat does not possess the essential requirements of a proper life-saving boat. Has the minister given us all the information he has as to the quality of these boats?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I fancy that some of the boats which are being built to-day for lifesaving purposes are better than those which have been in use at the life-saving stations for a great many years. We are trying, little by little, to substitute better boats for those now in use. I have heard no complaint about the Cape Tormentine boat.

My information is that there is a better type of boat in use in the United States. Why was the life-saving station at Souris removed from where it was to where it now is?
This station was established in 1908 and the boathouse built upon some land supposed to belong to Mr. J. J. Hughes, M.P., for which a nominal rental of $1 was to be paid by the department.
In 1911 it became necessary to enlarge the boathouse, and for this more land was required. When the matter was taken up it was discovered that the boathouse was not on Mr. Hughes' land at all, but partly on land belonging to the estate of the late John McPhee and partly on land owned by Mr. John McLean. Mr. Hughes then offered a new lease of right of way at and through his lane with a proviso allowing him to terminate said lease on six months' notice. It was impossible to accept this offer as, if the right of way was withdrawn there would be no way of getting the boat and wagon to the railway.
Mr. Lord, superintendent of life-saving station, after looking into the whole matter, recommended the purchase of a site from Mr. J. A. Remick, to which the boathouse could be movej

before the addition was built, and the matter would then be settled denitely. After approaching Mr. Remlclc, Mr. Lord was advised by Messrs, Fraser and McQuaid, attorneys, that the property in question was owned by the estate of John McPhee and could only be sold or leased after authority had been obtained from the Court of Chancery.
On this being reported to the department the chief engineer advised having the land expropriated, which was accordingly done. The cost of the land was $76, being 76 feet at $1 per foot frontage and the building was moved on to it at a cost of $70. After moving the building was reported to be in good shape. On the 17th of February 1914, however, the boathouse was damaged by an exceedingly heavy easterly gale which occurred on that day. It was then decided that the building had been placed too far forward when moved and it was accordingly moved back a little further where it now it.
My ihon. friend asked me about this and asked me to have the information when the Naval Estimates came up.
The boathouse was really on land belonging to the Crown.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That does not appear to have been the opinion.
At all events it was on land that belonged to the McPhee estate, nobody claimed it, nobody asked any price for it or asked rent.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Does my hon. friend know the firm of Murray and McQuaid ?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: They advised that the land belonged to the McPhee estate. The land where it was belonged to two people, McPhee and John McLean.
I do not think the report is correct. It really was very difficult to move the building.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It only cost $70.
The building had to be moved across a wharf, and it was injured in the moving, and it is not now in as good a site as before; it is not as well sheltered or so near to deep water.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The Teport from Mr. Lord, superintendent of life saving stations for Prince Edward Island, is as follows:
With reference to the question: " is the new situation preferable to the old one?" I beg to state that the present site is infinitely better than the former one on account of the protection given by whiarf property owned by Messrs. Matthew and McClean and the railway wharf property.
Mr. Lord was the man who selected the first site, and 'he thought it was the best ;in the harbour.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: He must have changed his mind.

I asked during the last regular session how it was that Quebec, one of the important maritime provinces of Canada, was without a life-saving 'Station, and the minister said he would look into the matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I have here a memorandum prepared by Admiral Kingsmill, in consequence of my hon. friend's request:
Memorandum for the Deputy Minister.
Regarding your request for a note giving reasons why there are no life saving stations on the river St. Lawrence: On the upper part of the St. Lawrence there is no necessity for any station, as vessels getting into difficulties are not likely to be completely wrecked so as to endanger the crew.
The lower part of the St. Lawrence is populated nearly all along its entire banks for a long way down, by farmers, etc., and If a small vessel is wrecked, until you get Into the gulf there are seldom heavy enough seas to break up a vessel before the persons on board could get ashore. I believe, several years ago it was proposed to erect a station in Chaleur bay but I can find no record of anything having been done.
As to establishing stations now on the lower part of the St. Lawrence and the gulf, I see less reason for it than in the past. At present, in the fishing communities there are so many large and well equipped motor boats that there would be no difficulty in getting men to go to a wreck if necessary, while the difficulty of proper supervision of a station districts is so great in these outlying districts. I could not recommend the establishment of them. .
There is no doubt a considerable feeling about, that had there been a life saving station in the vicinity more lives would have been saved when the Empress of Ireland sank off Father Point. A collision in open water is no reason for establishing life saving stations. Had there been a station near at hand it would have meant one more boat to assist in rescue work. The chances of collisions taking place in the vicinity of life saving stations are remote, it is impossible to provide against such accidents. That is Admiral Kingsmiill's opinion.
